editorialDecl.p: New English translation produced by the Falsafa project (Thothica) using an in-house agentic AI translation system, rendered from the Perseus source edition and reviewed by the project. Contributed to provide a translation for a work that previously had no English translation in the corpus.

div.p: It is my purpose to record the successions of the holy apostles, together with the times that have passed from our Saviour's day down to our own; the number and greatness of the deeds said to have been wrought in the history of the Church; the number of those who governed and presided over it with distinction in the most renowned communities; the number of those who in each generation, whether by the spoken or the written word, were ambassadors of the divine teaching; who, and how many, and at what times, driven by the lust of innovation to the extremity of error, proclaimed themselves the introducers of knowledge falsely so called, ravaging the flock of Christ without mercy, like grievous wolves;

Since in him there is a twofold nature—the one likened to the head, in which he is conceived as God, the other compared to the feet, in which for our salvation he put on a manhood subject to the same conditions as our own—our account of what follows will be complete if we begin the narrative of his whole history from the chief and most authoritative points of the doctrine. In this way also the antiquity and divine character of the Christian profession will be displayed to those who suppose it new and outlandish, appearing only yesterday and not before.
That the very name both of Jesus and indeed of Christ was held in honour among the God-beloved prophets themselves of old, it is now time to show.

Let these things, then, be set down by me here of necessity, before the history, lest anyone should suppose that our Saviour and Lord Jesus the Christ is recent because of the times of his life in the flesh. And lest anyone should imagine that his teaching too is new and strange, as composed by a man who was recent and in nothing differing from the rest of mankind, come, let us treat briefly of this also.

Come now, after the needful preparation for the ecclesiastical history we have set before us, let us at last set forth, as upon a kind of journey, beginning from the appearance of our Saviour in the flesh, having called upon God the Father of the Word, and the very Jesus Christ who has been declared, our Saviour and Lord, the heavenly Word of God, to be our helper and fellow-worker in the truth of the narrative.

At that time also, when Herod, the first of foreign race, had taken over the kingdom of the nation of the Jews, the prophecy delivered through Moses received its fulfilment, which declared that there should not fail a ruler from Judah, nor a leader from his loins, until he come for whom it is reserved—whom it also declares shall be the expectation of the nations.

Since both Matthew and Luke have delivered to us in their Gospels the genealogy of Christ in different ways, and they are thought by many to disagree, and each of the faithful, in ignorance of the truth, has been zealous to invent explanations of these passages, come, let us set forth the account concerning these matters which has come down to us, which Africanus, of whom we made mention a little before, recorded in a letter written to Aristides concerning the harmony of the genealogy in the Gospels. Having refuted the opinions of the rest as forced and false, he sets forth the account which he himself had received in these very words:

But when Christ had been born, in accordance with the prophecies, in Bethlehem of Judaea at the times indicated, Herod, on the inquiry of the Magi from the East, who asked where was he that was born King of the Jews—for they had seen his star, and this had been to them the cause of so long a journey, in their eagerness to worship as God the one who was born—was not a little disturbed at the matter, as supposing his rule to be in peril; and having inquired of the teachers of the law among the nation where they expected the Christ to be born, when he learned that the prophecy of Micah foretold it would be in Bethlehem, he commanded by a single edict that the infants in Bethlehem and in all its borders, from two years old and under, according to the time exactly ascertained by him from the Magi, should be put to death—supposing that Jesus too, as was likely, would share the same calamity with his coevals.

With the establishment of Archelaus in the rule after Herod, the historian above mentioned agrees, recording both the manner in which he succeeded to the kingdom over the Jews by the testaments of his father Herod and the decision of Caesar Augustus, and how, when after a ten-year period he fell from his rule, his brothers Philip and the younger Herod, together with Lysanias, governed their own tetrarchies.

In their time, then, according to the evangelist, when Tiberius Caesar was in the fifteenth year and Pontius Pilate in the fourth of his governorship, and when Herod and Lysanias and Philip were tetrarchs of the rest of Judaea, our Saviour and Lord Jesus, the Christ of God, being about thirty years old, came to the baptism of John, and then made the beginning of his preaching according to the Gospel.

Not long after, when John the Baptist had been beheaded by the younger Herod, the divine Scripture of the Gospels makes mention; and Josephus also bears witness with it, naming Herodias by name, and saying that Herod took her, the wife of his brother, to wife, having put away the woman who had first been lawfully married to him (this was the daughter of Aretas, king of the Petraeans), and having separated Herodias from her husband while he yet lived—on whose account he both slew John and took up war against Aretas, as one whose daughter had been dishonoured;

The naming of the apostles of the Saviour is clear to everyone from the Gospels; but of the seventy disciples no list anywhere is extant. It is said, at any rate, that one of them was Barnabas, of whom both the Acts of the Apostles have made mention in various places, and not least Paul writing to the Galatians. They say that Sosthenes too was of these, who wrote with Paul to the Corinthians;

The account concerning Thaddaeus was of this manner. The divinity of our Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ, being noised abroad among all men on account of his wonder-working power, drew countless multitudes even of those in foreign lands far from Judaea, in the hope of healing from diseases and sufferings of every kind.

Whatever it was needful, as in a preface, to set forth concerning the ecclesiastical history—both as to the divinity of the saving Word, and as to the antiquity of the doctrines of our teaching and the ancient origin of the evangelic polity of the Christians; and moreover whatever concerns his recent manifestation, the things before the Passion, and the matter of the choosing of the apostles—all this we have treated in the book before this, abridging the proofs.

First, then, in the place of the traitor Judas, Matthias is chosen by lot to the apostleship—he too being one, as has been shown, of the disciples of the Lord. And there are appointed, by prayer and the laying on of hands of the apostles, for the ministry of service for the common good, approved men, seven in number, those about Stephen. He too, first after the Lord, at the very time of his ordination, as though he had been advanced for this very thing, was stoned to death by the slayers of the Lord, and thus first bore away the crown, answering to his own name, of the worthy victors among the martyrs of Christ.

And now, when the marvellous resurrection of our Saviour and his ascension into the heavens had already become noised abroad among most men, and since an ancient custom had prevailed for the rulers of the nations to signify to him who held the imperial sway whatever was newly arising among them, that nothing might escape him of what was done, Pilate communicated to Tiberius the emperor the things concerning the resurrection of our Saviour Jesus from the dead, already noised abroad among all throughout all Palestine,

Thus, then, by the heavenly power and co-operation, the saving word, all at once, like a beam of the sun, illumined the whole world. Straightway, in accordance with the divine Scriptures, the voice of his inspired evangelists and apostles went forth into all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world.

Tiberius, then, having reigned about twenty-two years, died; and after him Gaius, taking over the government, straightway set the diadem on the head of Agrippa, the ruler of the Jews, making him king of the tetrarchy of Philip and of Lysanias; to which, after no long time, he delivered also the tetrarchy of Herod, punishing Herod (this was he of the time of the Saviour's Passion), together with his wife Herodias, with perpetual exile, for very many charges. Josephus is witness of these things too.

And indeed the things that befell the Jews in the time of Gaius he delivers in five books, recounting at once the madness of Gaius—how he proclaimed himself a god and committed countless outrages in his rule—and the miseries of the Jews under him, and the embassy which he himself undertook to the city of the Romans on behalf of his countrymen at Alexandria; and how, when he stood before Gaius on behalf of the ancestral laws, he carried away nothing but laughter and derision, and all but underwent the peril of his life.

And after the death of Tiberius, Gaius, taking over the rule, committed many outrages against many; but most of all he grievously injured the whole nation of the Jews. This it is possible to learn briefly from his own words, in which he writes thus:

It is worth not being ignorant that the account holds that even that very Pilate of the Saviour's time fell, in the reign of Gaius, whose times we are recounting, into such calamities that of necessity he became his own slayer and the avenger of himself by his own hand—the divine vengeance, as it seems, having pursued him not long after. This those of the Greeks relate who have recorded the Olympiads together with the deeds done in their times.
CHAPTER VIII

But Gaius, having held the rule not even four full years, was succeeded by the emperor Claudius; in whose time, a famine pressing upon the world (this even those writers far removed from our account have delivered in their histories), the prediction in the Acts of the Apostles of the prophet Agabus, that there should be a famine over all the world, received its fulfilment.
"Now about that time"—that is, plainly, the time under Claudius—"Herod the king laid hands on certain of the church to afflict them, and he slew James the brother of John with the sword."

But the things of the king's attempt against the apostles no longer admitted of delay; for straightway the avenging minister of the divine vengeance pursued him, immediately after his plot against the apostles, as the Scripture of the Acts relates—having set out for Caesarea, and there, on a notable festival day, arrayed in splendid and royal apparel, having made an oration on high before the tribunal; for, when all the people had acclaimed his oration as the voice of a god and not of a man, the oracle relates that straightway an angel of the Lord smote him, and that, being eaten of worms, he expired.

But since again Luke in the Acts brings in Gamaliel, in the deliberation concerning the apostles, saying that about the time indicated "rose up Theudas, saying that he himself was somebody, who was destroyed, and all, as many as obeyed him, were dispersed"—come, let us set forth also the writing of Josephus concerning this man. He relates, again in the same work of his just mentioned, these very things in these words:
"Moreover, the great famine also befell Judaea, in which queen Helena, having bought corn at much cost from Egypt, distributed it to the needy."

But now, as the faith in our Saviour and Lord Jesus Christ was already being spread among all men, the enemy of the salvation of men, contriving to seize beforehand the imperial city, leads thither Simon, before mentioned; and indeed, aiding the artful sorceries of the man, he appropriated to error very many of those dwelling in Rome.

Such evils' father and fashioner, Simon, at that time the evil power, hater of good and plotter against the salvation of men, set up as a great and mighty adversary of the inspired apostles of our Saviour.

Thus, then, when the divine word had come to dwell among them, the power of Simon was quenched, and straightway, together with the man himself, was undone. And so great a light of godliness shone upon the minds of the hearers of Peter that they were not content to be satisfied with hearing once, nor with the unwritten teaching of the divine preaching, but with all manner of entreaties besought Mark, whose Gospel is extant, being the follower of Peter, that he would leave them also a written memorial of the teaching delivered to them by word, and did not desist until they had prevailed upon the man; and thus they became the cause of the writing of the Gospel called according to Mark.
This Mark, they say, was the first to be sent to Egypt and to preach the Gospel which he himself had also composed, and the first to establish churches at Alexandria itself.

He, the account holds, came in the time of Claudius at Rome into conversation with Peter, who was then preaching to those there. And this would not be improbable, since the very work of which we speak, laboured upon by him later and after a length of time, plainly contains the rules of the church preserved even now and to our own day among us;

Copious indeed in language, and broad in thought, lofty and elevated as he was in his contemplations of the divine Scriptures, he made his exposition of the sacred discourses varied and manifold: on the one hand, going through the treatment of the matters in Genesis in connected sequence, in the works which he entitled Allegories of the Sacred Laws; on the other, having made, by separate divisions of chapters, the difficulties of the questions sought in the Scriptures, with their statements and solutions, in those works to which correspondingly he set the title Of the Questions and Solutions in Genesis and in Exodus.

While Claudius still administered the empire, at the festival of the Passover so great a sedition and tumult arose at Jerusalem that, of those alone who were pressed together by force about the exits of the temple, thirty thousand Jews perished, trodden down by one another; and the festival became a mourning to the whole nation, and a lamentation in every house. These things too in these words Josephus relates.
And under Nero, while Felix was procurator of Judaea, Josephus again in these very words thus writes of the sedition of the priests against one another, in the twentieth book of the Antiquities:

Next to these he adds, after other things, saying: "But with a greater blow than these did the Egyptian false prophet afflict the Jews. For there came into the country a man, a sorcerer, who put upon himself the credit of a prophet, and gathered about thirty thousand of the deceived, and leading them about from the wilderness to the mount called of Olives, he was able thence to break through into Jerusalem and, having overpowered both the Roman garrison and the people, to play the tyrant with the guards who had rushed in with him.

And Festus is sent by Nero as his successor; in whose time Paul, having pleaded his cause, is brought in bonds to Rome. Aristarchus was with him, whom in one of the epistles he fitly calls his fellow-prisoner. And Luke, who also delivered the Acts of the Apostles in writing, brought his history to an end at this point, noting that Paul spent two whole years at Rome at liberty, and preached the word of God without hindrance.

But the Jews, when Paul had appealed to Caesar and had been sent away by Festus to the city of the Romans, falling away from the hope by which they had laid their plot against him, turned against James the brother of the Lord, to whom the throne of the bishopric in Jerusalem had been entrusted by the apostles. Such are the things dared by them against him also.
In the eighth year of the reign of Nero, Annianus, first after Mark the evangelist, succeeded to the ministry of the community at Alexandria.
CHAPTER XXV

When now the rule of Nero was being firmly established, plunging into unholy practices, he armed himself even against the religion toward the God of all. To write what manner of man he was in wickedness would not belong to the present leisure;

Again Josephus, having gone through very many things concerning the calamity that overtook the whole nation of the Jews, declares in these words that, among very many others, countless of those honoured among the Jews, scourged and tortured, were crucified in Jerusalem itself by Florus; and that he was the procurator of Judaea when the beginning of the war was kindled, which happened in the twelfth year of the reign of Nero.

Such, then, were the things concerning the Jews. But the holy apostles and disciples of our Saviour being scattered over the whole world, Thomas, as the tradition holds, obtained Parthia by lot; Andrew, Scythia; John, Asia, with whom also he tarried, and died at Ephesus;

After the martyrdom of Paul and Peter, Linus was the first to be allotted the bishopric of the church of the Romans. Paul makes mention of him, writing to Timothy from Rome, in the salutation at the end of the epistle.
CHAPTER III

Of Peter, then, one epistle, that called his former, is acknowledged; and this the elders of old also used as indisputable in their own writings. But the so-called second we have received as not testamentary; nevertheless, having appeared useful to many, it was studied along with the other Scriptures.

That Paul, preaching to those of the nations, laid the foundations of the churches from Jerusalem and round about as far as Illyricum, would be evident both from his own words and from what Luke related in the Acts;

After Nero had held the rule thirteen years, and after the affairs of Galba and Otho had occupied a year and six months, Vespasian, distinguished by his campaigns against the Jews, was proclaimed emperor in Judaea itself, hailed as imperator by the armies there. Having forthwith set out for Rome, he entrusted to his son Titus the war against the Jews.

Come, then, take again the fifth book of the Histories of Josephus in hand, and go through the tragedy of the things then done. "To the well-to-do," he says, "even to remain was equal to destruction; for under pretext of desertion one would be slain for the sake of his property. With the famine the frenzy of the seditious increased, and day by day both terrors were the more kindled.

Such were the requitals of the Jews' transgression and impiety against the Christ of God; and it is fitting to set beside them the unerring prediction of our Saviour, by which he declares these very things, prophesying somewhat thus: "But woe to those who are with child and to those who give suck in those days; and pray that your flight be not in winter, neither on a sabbath. For there shall be then great tribulation, such as was not from the beginning of the world until now, nor ever shall be."

So then, take and read the things declared by him in the sixth book of the Histories, in these words: "The wretched people, then, the deceivers and those who lied against God at that time misled; but to the clear portents that foreshowed the coming desolation they neither gave heed nor believed, but, as though thunderstruck, and having neither eyes nor soul, they paid no regard to the proclamations of God—

After all these things, it is right not to be ignorant even concerning Josephus himself, who has contributed so much to the history in hand, whence and from what race he sprang. He shows this too, saying thus: "Josephus, son of Matthias, a priest from Jerusalem, who himself at the first warred against the Romans, and of necessity was present at the later events."
"There are not, then, among us myriads of discordant and conflicting books, but only two-and-twenty, containing the record of all time, justly believed divine.

Let us pass to what follows. After the martyrdom of James and the capture of Jerusalem that came straightway after, the account holds that those of the apostles and of the disciples of the Lord still surviving in life came together from everywhere to the same place, along with the kinsmen of the Lord after the flesh (for many of these too were still surviving in life), and all of them together took counsel as to whom it was meet to judge worthy of the succession of James; and, with one mind, all approved Symeon the son of Clopas, of whom the Scripture of the Gospel also makes mention, as worthy of the throne of the community there—being, as they say, a cousin of the Saviour; for Hegesippus relates that Clopas was a brother of Joseph.
CHAPTER XII

And besides these things, that Vespasian, after the capture of Jerusalem, commanded that all of David's family should be sought out, that none of the royal tribe might be left among the Jews; and that a very great persecution again hung over the Jews from this cause.
CHAPTER XIII

When Vespasian had reigned ten years, the emperor Titus, his son, succeeded him; in the second year of whose reign Linus, bishop of the church of the Romans, having held the ministry for twelve years, delivered it to Anencletus. And Titus was succeeded by his brother Domitian, after he had reigned two years and the like number of months.
CHAPTER XIV
In the fourth year of Domitian, the first of the community at Alexandria, Annianus, having completed two-and-twenty years, died; and the second, Abilius, succeeded him.
CHAPTER XV

And in the twelfth year of the same reign, Clement succeeded Anencletus, who had been bishop of the church of the Romans twelve years; whom the apostle, writing to the Philippians, teaches to have been his fellow-worker, saying: "with Clement also and the rest of my fellow-workers, whose names are in the book of life."
CHAPTER XVI

Of this man, then, one acknowledged epistle is extant, great and marvellous, which he drew up as from the church of the Romans to that of the Corinthians, a sedition having then arisen at Corinth. This we know to have been publicly read in very many churches before the congregation, both in old times and in our own. And that the matter of the Corinthian sedition was stirred up in his time, Hegesippus is a trustworthy witness.
CHAPTER XVII

Domitian, having shown much cruelty toward many, and having slain not a few of the well-born and notable men at Rome without reasonable judgement, and having punished countless other illustrious men, without cause, with exiles beyond the frontier and with the loss of their properties, at last established himself as a successor to the enmity against God and warfare against God of Nero. He, then, was the second to stir up the persecution against us, although his father Vespasian had devised nothing amiss against us.
CHAPTER XVIII
At this time the account holds that the apostle and at once evangelist John, still surviving in life, was condemned to dwell on the island of Patmos for the sake of his testimony to the divine word.

And when the same Domitian commanded that those of David's line be slain, an ancient account holds that certain of the heretics accused the descendants of Jude (and this man was a brother after the flesh of the Saviour) as being of David's line and as bearing kinship to Christ himself. These things Hegesippus declares in these very words, saying somewhat thus.
CHAPTER XX

"Now there yet survived of the family of the Lord the grandsons of Jude, who was called his brother after the flesh; whom they informed against as being of David's line. These the evocatus brought to Domitian Caesar; for he feared the coming of Christ, as Herod also did.

Nerva, having reigned a little more than a year, was succeeded by Trajan; whose first year it was in which Cerdo succeeded Abilius, who had governed the community at Alexandria for thirteen years; he was the third to preside over those there after the first, Annianus. In this time Clement was still governing the Romans, holding likewise the third place of those who had been bishops there after Paul and Peter; Linus was the first, and after him Anencletus.
CHAPTER XXII

But of those at Antioch also, Euodius having been appointed first, Ignatius was known as the second in the times indicated. Symeon likewise, the second after the brother of our Saviour, held the ministry of the church in Jerusalem in these times.
CHAPTER XXIII

At this time there was still surviving in Asia the very one whom Jesus loved, apostle and at once evangelist, John, who governed the churches there, having returned from his exile on the island after the death of Domitian.
Come now, let us note the indisputable writings of this apostle also.

It is reasonable, having come to this point, to recapitulate the writings of the New Testament that have been indicated. And first must be ranged the holy tetrad of the Gospels, which the writing of the Acts of the Apostles follows;

Let us pass now to what follows of the history. Menander, having succeeded Simon Magus, is shown to be a second weapon of the diabolical working, no worse than the former, in manner. He too was a Samaritan, and, having advanced to the height of sorcery no less than his teacher, he lavished greater marvel-mongerings, saying of himself that he was the Saviour sent down from above somewhere, from the invisible ages, for the salvation of men;

Others, whom the evil demon, being unable to shake from their disposition toward the Christ of God, finding seized on the other side, he appropriated; the first members fitly named these Ebionites, who held poor and lowly opinions concerning Christ.

In the times indicated we have received that Cerinthus became the author of another heresy. Gaius, whose words I have already before set down, in the disputation ascribed to him writes thus concerning him:

At this time too the so-called heresy of the Nicolaitans subsisted for a very short while, of which indeed the Apocalypse of John makes mention. These boasted of Nicolaus, one of those about Stephen who had been chosen by the apostles for the care of the needy. But Clement of Alexandria, in the third book of the Stromateis, relates these things concerning him in these words:

But Clement, whose words we have just read, after the foregoing, reckons up, against those who reject marriage, the apostles who were proved in wedlock, saying: "Or will they even reject the apostles? For Peter and Philip begat children, and Philip even gave his daughters in marriage to husbands; and Paul does not hesitate, in a certain epistle, to address his consort, whom he did not carry about because of the convenience of his ministry."

Of Paul and Peter, then, both the time and the manner of their death, and moreover the place of the deposition of their tabernacles after their departure from life, have already been shown by us before;

After Nero and Domitian, in the time of him whose times we are now examining, the account holds that the persecution against us was stirred up partially and by cities, from the risings of the populace; in which Symeon the son of Clopas, whom we showed to have been appointed second bishop of the church in Jerusalem, we have received departed life by martyrdom.

So great, however, was the persecution against us then intensified in very many places, that Pliny Secundus, a most distinguished of governors, moved by the multitude of the martyrs, communicated to the emperor concerning the multitude of those slain for the faith; and at the same time he made known that he had detected them in nothing unholy nor contrary to the laws, save only that, rising at dawn, they hymned Christ as a god; but that adultery and murder and the kindred unlawful offences they themselves too forbade, and did all things in accordance with the laws.

Of the bishops at Rome, in the third year of the reign of the aforesaid emperor, Clement, having delivered the ministry to Evarestus, departed life, having presided in all over the teaching of the divine word for nine years.
CHAPTER XXXV

But when Symeon also had been perfected in the manner shown, a certain Jew, Justus by name, succeeded to the throne of the bishopric in Jerusalem—he himself too being one of the countless multitude of those of the circumcision who at that time had believed in Christ.
CHAPTER XXXVI
There was distinguished in these times in Asia Polycarp, a companion of the apostles, who had been entrusted with the bishopric of the church in Smyrna by the eyewitnesses and ministers of the Lord;

Of those who shone in these times was Quadratus also, whom, along with the daughters of Philip, the account holds to have been distinguished by the prophetic gift; and many others besides these were known in these times, holding the first rank of the succession of the apostles; who also, being such God-befitting disciples, built upon the foundations of the churches laid everywhere by the apostles, increasing yet more the preaching and sowing broadcast the saving seeds of the kingdom of the heavens throughout the whole world.

As, indeed, in the epistles of Ignatius which we enumerated, and in that of Clement acknowledged by all, which he drew up from the person of the church of the Romans to that of the Corinthians; in which, having set down many thoughts of the epistle to the Hebrews, and having even used some sayings from it verbatim,

The acknowledged writing of Clement, then, is manifest; and the things of Ignatius and Polycarp have been spoken of. Of Papias five writings in number are extant, which are entitled Expositions of the Oracles of the Lord. Of these Irenaeus too makes mention as the only ones written by him, saying somewhat thus: "These things Papias too, a hearer of John, and a companion of Polycarp, an ancient man, attests in writing in the fourth of his own books. For there are five books composed by him."

About the twelfth year of the reign of Trajan, the bishop of the community in Alexandria, indicated by us a little before, departed life, and Primus, fourth from the apostles, was allotted the ministry of those there. At this time also Alexander, at Rome, when Evarestus had completed eight years, took over the bishopric, tracing the fifth succession from Peter and Paul.
CHAPTER II

And while the things of our Saviour's teaching and of his church, flourishing day by day, advanced to greater increase, the things of the Jews' calamity were at their height with successive ills. Already, then, as the emperor was driving on into the eighteenth year, again a rising of the Jews, breaking out, destroyed a very great multitude of them.

When Trajan had held the rule for twenty whole years lacking six months, Aelius Hadrian succeeded to the government. To him Quadratus addressed and presented a discourse, having composed an apology on behalf of our religion, because certain wicked men were attempting to molest our people; and the work is still extant among very many of the brethren, and indeed among us; from which it is possible to behold clear proofs both of the man's understanding and of his apostolic correctness.

In the third year of the same reign, Alexander, bishop of the Romans, died, having completed the tenth year of his stewardship; Xystus was his successor. And of the community of the Alexandrians, about the same time, Primus, having departed in the twelfth year of his presidency, was succeeded by Justus.
CHAPTER V
Having by no means found the times of the bishops in Jerusalem preserved in writing—for the account holds that they were exceedingly short-lived—

And indeed, the revolt of the Jews having again advanced to a great and considerable pitch, Rufus, prefect of Judaea, a military force having been sent him by the emperor, prosecuting their frenzies without sparing, destroyed by myriads at once men together with children and women, and by the law of war reduced their lands to slavery.

Now while the churches throughout the world were shining like the most brilliant luminaries, and the faith in our Saviour and Lord Jesus Christ was flourishing among the whole race of men, the hater-of-good demon, as the enemy of truth and ever the most hostile to the salvation of men, turning all his devices against the church, of old armed himself against it with persecutions from without;
Among these was known Hegesippus, whose words we have already before very often used, having set down from his tradition certain things of the apostolic times.

"To Minucius Fundanus. I received a letter written to me from Serennius Granianus, a most illustrious man, whom you succeeded. It does not seem to me, then, that the matter should be left uninvestigated, that the men may not be disturbed, nor occasion of mischief be afforded to the calumniators.

When this man had paid his debt after twenty-one years, Antoninus, called the Pious, succeeded to the rule of the Romans. In his first year Telesphorus departed life in the eleventh year of his ministry, and Hyginus received the lot of the bishopric of the Romans. Irenaeus, however, relates that Telesphorus was distinguished by a martyr's death, showing at the same time that in the time of the said Roman bishop Hyginus, Valentinus, the introducer of his own heresy, and Cerdo, the author of the error of Marcion, were both known at Rome; and he writes thus:
CHAPTER XI

"For Valentinus came to Rome in the time of Hyginus, flourished under Pius, and remained until Anicetus; and Cerdo, the predecessor of Marcion, himself too in the time of Hyginus, who was the ninth bishop, having come to the church and made confession, so continued, now teaching in secret, now again making confession, now being convicted of the things which he wrongly taught, and withdrawing from the company of the brethren."

"To the Emperor Titus Aelius Hadrianus Antoninus Pius Caesar Augustus, and to Verissimus his son, a philosopher, and to Lucius, by nature son of the philosopher Caesar and adopted son of Pius, a lover of learning, and to the sacred senate and the whole people of the Romans, on behalf of those of every race of men unjustly hated and ill-treated, I, Justin, son of Priscus, son of Bacchius, of those from Flavia Neapolis of Syria Palestine, being one of them, have made this address and petition." And this same emperor, being petitioned also by other brethren of Asia, who were oppressed by the natives of the country with all manner of outrages, deemed the assembly of Asia worthy of such an ordinance:
CHAPTER XIII
"The Emperor Caesar Marcus Aurelius Antoninus Augustus, Armenicus, supreme high priest, holding the tribunician power for the fifteenth time, consul for the third, to the assembly of Asia, greeting.

In the times indicated, while Anicetus was governing the church of the Romans, Polycarp, still surviving in life, came to Rome and came into conference with Anicetus about a certain question concerning the day of the Passover, as Irenaeus relates.

At this time, very great persecutions having disturbed Asia, Polycarp was perfected by martyrdom; and I think it most necessary to set down his end, still extant in writing, in the memory of this history.

In these times also Justin, indicated by us a little before, having given a second book on behalf of our doctrines to the rulers indicated, is adorned with a divine martyrdom, the philosopher Crescens (this man emulated a life and manner answering to the title of Cynic) having contrived the plot against him; since, having often convicted him in disputations in the presence of hearers, at last he bound on himself the prize of victory of the truth of which he was an ambassador, through the martyrdom in his case.
The same man, before his own contest, makes mention in the former Apology of others who had been martyred before him, usefully to the subject relating these things also; and he writes thus:

This man has left us very many memorials of an educated mind, zealous about divine things, full of all profit; to which we shall refer the studious, having usefully noted those that have come to our knowledge.

And now, the said reign being driven on into its eighth year, Soter succeeded Anicetus, who had held the bishopric of the church of the Romans for eleven years in all; and likewise, Celadion having presided over the community of the Alexandrians for fourteen years,
CHAPTER XX

Agrippinus received the succession; and of the church of the Antiochenes Theophilus, sixth from the apostles, was known, Cornelius having been appointed fourth of those there after Hero, and after him Eros having succeeded to the bishopric in the fifth degree.
CHAPTER XXI

There flourished in these times in the church Hegesippus, whom we know from what precedes, and Dionysius bishop of the Corinthians, and Pinytus another, bishop of those in Crete, and Philip besides these, and Apolinarius and Melito and Musanus and Modestus, and above all Irenaeus; from whom the orthodoxy of the sound faith, of the apostolic tradition, has come down to us in writing.
CHAPTER XXII

Hegesippus, then, in the five memoirs that have come down to us, has left a most full record of his own mind; in which he shows that he met with very many bishops, having made a journey as far as Rome, and that he received the same teaching from all. It is possible, at any rate, to hear, after certain things said by him concerning the epistle of Clement to the Corinthians, that he adds these things:

And first concerning Dionysius it must be said that he was entrusted with the throne of the bishopric of the community in Corinth, and that, of his divine diligence, he imparted ungrudgingly, not only to those under him, but already also to those of foreign lands, by epistles, making himself most useful to all, in those catholic letters which he framed to the churches;

Of Theophilus, whom we have shown to be bishop of the church of the Antiochenes, three elementary writings to Autolycus are extant, and another bearing the title Against the Heresy of Hermogenes, in which he has used testimonies from the Apocalypse of John; and certain other catechetical books of his are extant. And since the heretics then too, no less, like tares, were spoiling the pure seed of the apostolic teaching, the shepherds of the churches everywhere, as though scaring off certain wild beasts from the sheep of Christ, kept them away, now by admonitions and exhortations to the brethren, now stripping more bare against them, by unwritten face-to-face disputations and refutations, and already also by written memoirs setting straight their opinions with most accurate proofs. And Theophilus, who with the rest campaigned against these, is plainly seen from a certain discourse not ignobly laboured by him against Marcion, which itself too, with the others we have mentioned, has been preserved to this day. Him, then, Maximinus, seventh from the apostles, succeeded in the church of the Antiochenes.
CHAPTER XXV

Philip, however, whom we knew from the words of Dionysius to be bishop of the community in Gortyna, has himself too composed a very diligent discourse against Marcion, and Irenaeus likewise, and Modestus, who also, beyond the rest, detected the man's error and brought it manifest to all; and many others besides, whose labours are preserved among very many of the brethren even to this day.
CHAPTER XXVI

In their time also Melito, bishop of the community in Sardis, and Apolinarius, of that in Hierapolis, flourished with distinction; who also each privately addressed discourses of apology on behalf of the faith to the emperor of the Romans of that time indicated.

Of Apolinarius, many being preserved among many, these are those that have come to us: the discourse to the aforesaid emperor, and the five writings To the Greeks, and On Truth, two books, and To the Jews, two; and the things which after these he composed against the heresy of the Phrygians, innovated not long after, but then beginning, as it were, to sprout up, while Montanus, together with his false prophetesses, was making the beginnings of his deviation.
CHAPTER XXVIII

And of Musanus, whom we reckoned among the foregoing, a most persuasive discourse is extant, written by him to certain brethren who had turned aside to the heresy of the so-called Encratites, then just beginning to sprout up and to introduce into life a strange and corrupting false opinion;
CHAPTER XXIX

of which deviation the account holds that Tatian was the author, whose words concerning the marvellous Justin we set down a little before, relating him to have been a disciple of the martyr. And Irenaeus shows this in the first book Against the Heresies, writing thus at once concerning him and concerning the heresy of his:

And in the same reign, the heresies multiplying in Mesopotamia, Bardesanes, a most able man and most skilled in disputation in the Syrian tongue, having composed dialogues against those of Marcion and certain others who presided over diverse doctrines, delivered them in his own tongue and writing, together with very many other writings of his; which his acquaintances (and there were very many of them, since he was powerful in argument) translated from the Syrian into the Greek tongue;

Soter, the bishop of the church of the Romans, having governed for eight years, ended his life; him Eleutherus, twelfth from the apostles, succeeded, in the seventeenth year of the emperor Antoninus Verus. In his time, the persecution against us being more violently kindled in certain parts of the earth from the rising of the populaces in the cities, it is possible to gather by conjecture, from the things that befell in one single nation, that myriads of martyrs were distinguished; which things it befell to be delivered in writing to those who came after, as being truly worthy of unfading memory.

Gaul, then, was the country in which the stadium of the said persons was set; the renowned and notable metropoleis of which, surpassing the rest of those there, are Lugdunum and Vienna, through both of which the river Rhone, flowing around the whole country with a great stream, passes.

Such were the things that befell the churches of Christ in the time of the said emperor, from which it is possible by reasonable conjecture to gather also the things wrought in the rest of the provinces. It is worth attaching to these, from the same writing, other words, in which the gentleness and loving-kindness of the said martyrs is recorded in these very words:
The same writing of the aforesaid martyrs contains also another story worthy of memory, which there could be no grudging in setting forth for the knowledge of those who shall read; and it is thus.

The same martyrs commended Irenaeus, who was then already a presbyter of the community at Lugdunum, to the said bishop at Rome, bearing very much witness to the man, as the words which run thus declare:

The account holds that the brother of this man, Marcus Aurelius Caesar, drawing up against the Germans and Sarmatians in battle, his army being pressed by thirst, was in helplessness; but that the soldiers of the so-called Melitene legion—a legion which from then to this day has subsisted through faith—in the array against the enemy bent the knee to the ground, after our own custom of prayers, and turned to supplications to God;
"The blessed apostles, then, having founded and built up the church, entrusted to Linus the ministry of the bishopric; of this Linus Paul makes mention in the epistles to Timothy.

These things Irenaeus, in accordance with the histories already gone through by us, set down in the works which he entitled, five in number, Of the Refutation and Overthrow of the Knowledge Falsely so Called; and in the second of the same work he indicates that even down to his time examples of the divine and marvellous power had been left in certain churches, in these words, saying:

Since at the beginning of the work we made a promise to set down in due season the words of the ancient ecclesiastical presbyters and writers, in which they have delivered in writing the traditions that came down to them concerning the testamentary Scriptures, and Irenaeus was one of these, come, let us set down his words also,

Antoninus having continued in the reign nineteen years, Commodus took over the government; in whose first year Julian is entrusted with the bishopric of the churches at Alexandria, Agrippinus having completed the ministry for twelve years.
CHAPTER X

There presided then over the community of the faithful there a man most distinguished for learning, his name Pantaenus, a school of the sacred discourses subsisting among them from ancient custom; which extends also to us, and which we have received to be maintained by those powerful in word and in zeal concerning divine things; and especially at that season the said man is said to have shone, having set out from the philosophic school of those called Stoics.
In his time Clement was known at Alexandria, exercising himself in the divine Scriptures, of the same name as the one who of old governed the church of the Romans, a disciple of the apostles;

In their time the bishop of the church in Jerusalem was Narcissus, renowned among many even to this day, holding the fifteenth succession from the siege of the Jews under Hadrian, from which time, as we have shown, the church there first consisted of the nations after those of the circumcision, and Mark first of the nations governed them as bishop;

In this time also Rhodo, of those of Asian race, having been a disciple at Rome, as he himself relates, of Tatian, whom we have known from what precedes, having composed diverse books, with the rest is arrayed also against the heresy of Marcion; which he relates to have been divided into diverse opinions in his time, recording those who had brought in the division, and exactly refuting the false reasonings devised by each of these. Hear, then, him too writing these things:

But the enemy of the church of God, being especially a hater of good and a lover of wickedness, leaving no manner of plot against men untried, again set strange heresies to spring up against the church; of whom some, like venomous serpents, crept through Asia and Phrygia, boasting of Montanus indeed as the Advocate, and of the women from him, Priscilla and Maximilla, as having become prophetesses of Montanus.
CHAPTER XV

And others flourished at Rome, of whom Florinus was leader, having fallen from the presbytery of the church, and Blastus with him, held by a like fall; who also, drawing away many of the church, brought them under their own will, each trying privately to innovate concerning the truth.
CHAPTER XVI

Against the so-called heresy of the Phrygians, then, the power that champions the truth raised up at Hierapolis Apolinarius, of whom the account has before made mention, as a strong and irresistible weapon, and others with him, more of the learned men of that time; from whom there has been left to us also very much material of history.

And in this work he makes mention also of the writer Miltiades, as having himself too written a certain discourse against the aforesaid heresy; having set down certain of their words, he adds, saying: "Having found these things in a certain work of theirs in which they were opposing the work of our brother Alcibiades, in which he shows that a prophet ought not to speak in ecstasy, I made an abridgement."

Apollonius too, an ecclesiastical writer, having set himself to refute the so-called heresy of the Phrygians while it was still flourishing in Phrygia, made a special work against them, convicting verbatim their so-called prophecies as being false, and refuting what manner of life the leaders of the heresy had. Hear him, then, in these very words saying these things concerning Montanus:

Of the writings of Apolinarius against the said heresy, Serapion makes mention, who, the account holds, became bishop of the church of the Antiochenes in the times indicated after Maximinus; he makes mention of him in his own epistle to Caricus and Pontius, in which, himself too setting straight the same heresy, he adds these things:

Against those at Rome who corrupted the sound ordinance of the church, Irenaeus composed diverse epistles, the one entitled To Blastus, On Schism, the other To Florinus, On Monarchy, or That God is not the Author of Evils. For this opinion Florinus seemed to champion; on whose account, when he was again being drawn away by the error of Valentinus, the work On the Ogdoad too was composed by Irenaeus, in which he also indicates that he had received the first succession of the apostles;

In the same time of the reign of Commodus, our affairs were changed to gentleness, peace, with the divine grace, possessing the churches throughout the whole world; when the saving word was leading every soul of every race of men to the godly worship of the God of all, so that already even more of those at Rome distinguished for wealth and birth advanced toward their own salvation with their whole households and all their kin.

In the tenth year of the reign of Commodus, Eleutherus, having ministered the bishopric for thirteen years, was succeeded by Victor; in whose time also, Julian having completed his tenth year, Demetrius was entrusted with the ministry of the communities at Alexandria; in whose time also, of the church of the Antiochenes, the eighth from the apostles, Serapion already before declared, was still then known as bishop. And of Caesarea of Palestine Theophilus was governor, and Narcissus likewise, of whom the account before made mention, still then held the ministry of the church in Jerusalem; and of Corinth of Greece in the same time the bishop was Bacchyllus, and of the community in Ephesus Polycrates. And others, as is likely, besides these, countless, were distinguished in these times; but those of whom the orthodoxy of the faith has come down to us in writing, these we have reasonably enumerated by name.
CHAPTER XXIII

No small question being then stirred up, because the communities of all Asia thought, as from a more ancient tradition, that they ought to observe the fourteenth of the moon at the feast of the saving Passover, on which it was proclaimed to the Jews to sacrifice the lamb, so that it was needful by all means, on this day, on whatever day of the week it might fall, to make the dissolutions of the fasts—it not being the custom to perform it in this manner in the churches throughout all the rest of the world, which observed, from apostolic tradition, the custom that has prevailed even to this day, so that it is not fitting to dissolve the fasts on any other day than that of the resurrection of our Saviour—

And of these the determination was one, the one declared; but of the bishops in Asia, who strongly maintained that it was needful to preserve the custom of old delivered to them, the leader was Polycrates; who himself too, in the writing which he addressed to Victor and the church of the Romans, sets forth the tradition that had come to him, in these words:

Those, indeed, in Palestine, whom we have just gone through, Narcissus and Theophilus, and with them Cassius bishop of the church in Tyre, and Clarus of that in Ptolemais, and those who came together with these, having treated very much concerning the tradition concerning the Passover that had come down to them by succession from the apostles, at the end of the writing add these things in these very words: "Try to send copies of our epistle to every community, that we may not be liable to those who lightly deceive their own souls. And we declare to you that in Alexandria too they keep the same day as we do; for letters are carried from us to them and from them to us, so that with one accord and together we keep the holy day."
CHAPTER XXVI

But besides the works of Irenaeus rendered above, and his epistles, there is extant a certain very concise and most necessary discourse of his to the Greeks, entitled On Knowledge, and another, which he dedicated to a brother named Marcianus, For the Demonstration of the Apostolic Preaching, and a certain book of diverse discourses, in which he makes mention of the epistle to the Hebrews and of the so-called Wisdom of Solomon, setting down certain sayings from them. And the works of Irenaeus that have come to our knowledge are so many. Commodus having ended the rule after thirteen years, the emperor Severus, after the death of Commodus, Pertinax having continued not even six full months, holds power.
CHAPTER XXVII

Very many memorials, then, of the virtuous zeal of the ancient and ecclesiastical men of that time are preserved even now among many; of which, indeed, such as we ourselves have come to know, would be the works of Heraclitus on the apostle, and those of Maximus on the much-discussed question among the heretics, whence is evil, and concerning the doctrine that matter is created; and those of Candidus on the Hexaemeron, and of Apion on the same subject; likewise of Sextus on the resurrection, and another treatise of Arabianus, and of countless others, of whom, because we have no occasion, it is not possible either to deliver in writing the times or to note any mention of history. And the discourses of very many others too came to us, of whom it is not possible for us to enumerate even the names, of orthodox and ecclesiastical men, as indeed the interpretation of divine Scripture in each shows, but nevertheless unknown to us, because they do not bear the name of those who composed them.
CHAPTER XXVIII

In a certain work of one of these, laboured against the heresy of Artemon, which Paul of Samosata in our time has again attempted to renew, there is borne a certain narrative pertinent to the histories we are examining.

When Severus too was stirring up persecution against the churches, splendid martyrdoms of the champions of true religion were accomplished in every place, but most abundantly at Alexandria. Thither, as to a vast arena of the athletes of God, were sent forward those from Egypt and the whole of the Thebaid, and through their most steadfast endurance of manifold tortures and forms of death they won the crowns laid up with God. Among them was Leonides, called the father of Origen, who was beheaded and left behind his son, then quite young. It will not be out of place to relate briefly the disposition the boy displayed from that time toward the divine word, since the account commonly told of him is widely noised abroad among the multitude.

Much indeed might one say in attempting to hand down in writing, at leisure, the life of the man, and the composition concerning him would require a treatise of its own. Nevertheless we for the present, abridging most of it as briefly as we can, shall pass over a few particulars about him, drawing the matters here set forth from certain letters and from the account of those of his acquaintances whose lives have been preserved down to our own day. 2. The things concerning Origen even, so to speak, from his very swaddling-clothes seem to me worthy of record. It was the tenth year of the reign of Severus; Laetus was governor of Alexandria and the rest of Egypt, and Demetrius had but lately, after Julian, undertaken the oversight of the communities there. 3. When, therefore, the fire of persecution was kindled to a great height and countless numbers were being adorned with the crowns of martyrdom, so great a longing for martyrdom possessed the soul of Origen, while still quite a boy, that he made for the perils, eager to leap forward and rush into the contest. 4. Indeed, the term of his departure from life was already brought not far off, had not the divine and heavenly Providence, for the benefit of the many, opposed his eagerness through his mother. 5. She at first entreated him with words, begging him to spare her motherly feeling toward him; but when she saw that his ardour was the more intense, once he had learned that his father was taken and held in prison and had become wholly given over to the impulse toward martyrdom, she hid all his clothing and so laid upon him the necessity of remaining at home. 6. And he, since nothing else was left him to do, his eagerness being kindled beyond his years and not allowing him to be at rest, sent his father a most encouraging letter on martyrdom, in which he exhorted him in these very words: 'Take heed not to change your mind on our account.' Let this stand as a recorded proof of Origen's boyish shrewdness and of his most genuine disposition toward the fear of God. 7. For already he had laid down no small foundations in the words of the faith, having been trained in the divine Scriptures from earliest childhood. Indeed, he had laboured over these not moderately, his father, besides the ordinary course of education, having made these too the object of no incidental care. 8. Above all things, before the study of the Greek learning, he led him to be exercised in the sacred studies, exacting from him daily memorizations and recitations. 9. Nor were these things irksome to the boy, but he laboured at them with the utmost eagerness, so that the simple and ready readings of the sacred words did not satisfy him; he sought something further, and even from that age busied himself with deeper speculations, so that he gave trouble to his father by inquiring what could be the meaning of the inspired Scripture. 10. His father, to his face, would seemingly rebuke him, exhorting him to seek nothing beyond his years nor beyond the obvious sense; but privately within himself he rejoiced greatly and gave the greatest thanks to God, the author of all good things, that He had deemed him worthy to become the father of such a child. 11. They say that often, standing over the boy as he slept, he would bare his breast, and, as though a divine Spirit were enshrined within it, would kiss it reverently and count himself blessed in his goodly offspring. These and other things akin to them they record of Origen while he was a boy. 12. When his father had been perfected by martyrdom, he was left bereft, together with his mother and six younger brothers, being not yet a full seventeen years old. 13. His father's property having been confiscated to the imperial treasury, he was reduced with his kindred to want of the necessaries of life. Yet he was deemed worthy of God's care, and met with welcome and rest at the house of a woman very wealthy and otherwise most distinguished, who was, however, entertaining a man notorious among the heretics then at Alexandria. This man was an Antiochene by birth; the woman aforesaid kept him with her as an adopted son and treated him with the highest regard. 14. But Origen, though compelled to consort with him, gave clear proofs of his orthodoxy in the faith from that time. For although a great multitude—not only of heretics but also of our own people—gathered about Paul (for that was the man's name) on account of his seeming proficiency in argument, Origen was never induced to join with him in prayer, keeping from childhood the rule of the Church, and abhorring, as he himself somewhere says in these very words, the teachings of the heresies. 15. Having been advanced by his father in the Greek learning, and after his father's death applying himself the more ardently to the discipline of letters, he had so prepared himself in grammatical studies that, not long after his father's perfecting, by devoting himself to these, he was abundantly supplied with the necessaries, as far as his age allowed.

While he was thus engaged in teaching, as he himself records in writing, and there was no one at Alexandria devoted to catechizing—all having been driven away by the threat of persecution—some of the heathen came to him to hear the word of God. 2. The first of these, he notes, was Plutarch, who, after living well, was adorned with a divine martyrdom; the second, Heraclas, Plutarch's brother, who himself also, having furnished with him abundant proof of a philosophic life and discipline, was deemed worthy of the bishopric of Alexandria after Demetrius. 3. He was in his eighteenth year when he took charge of the catechetical school; and he advanced in it during the persecutions under Aquila the governor of Alexandria, when especially he won a most renowned name among all who set out from the faith, by the welcome and ready zeal which he showed toward all the holy martyrs, both unknown and known. 4. For not only was he with the holy martyrs while in bonds, and while under examination up to the final sentence, but also after this, when they were led away to death, employing great boldness and coming to close grips with the dangers; so that, as he advanced courageously and greeted the martyrs with much boldness by a kiss, the heathen mob standing round him, in their fury, more than once all but stoned him to death, had he not, finding the divine right hand again and again his helper, marvellously escaped. 5. And the same divine and heavenly grace guarded him at other times—again and again, more times than one can tell—when on account of his exceeding eagerness and boldness for the word of Christ he was plotted against. So great was the war of the unbelievers against him that, forming bands, they set soldiers about the house in which he dwelt, on account of the multitude of those being instructed by him in the sacred faith. 6. Thus daily was the persecution against him kindled, so that the whole city could no longer hold him; he changed from house to house, driven from every quarter, on account of the multitude of those who through him came to the divine teaching. For his very works in practice held the achievements of a most genuine philosophy, exceedingly admirable. 7. For 'as was his word, such,' they say, 'was his manner of life; and as his manner of life, such was his word,' as he displayed; on which account especially, the divine power working with him, he led countless numbers to his own zeal. 8. When he saw that yet more pupils were coming to him, the work of catechizing having been committed to him alone by Demetrius, who presided over the church, he judged the teaching of grammatical studies discordant with the discipline of the divine learning, and without delay he broke off the teaching of grammar as unprofitable and contrary to the sacred studies. 9. Then, by a fitting reasoning, that he might not be in need of help from others, he handed over whatever volumes of ancient literature he formerly possessed, beautifully written and carefully prepared, and was content with four obols a day brought to him by the one who had purchased them. For very many years he continued to practise philosophy in this manner, stripping from himself all the materials of youthful desires; through every day he filled up no small toils of discipline, and during the greater part of the night devoted himself to the study of the divine Scriptures, persevering as far as possible in a most philosophic life—now in exercises of fasting, now in measured spans of sleep, which he was zealous to take not at all upon a couch but upon the bare ground. 10. Above all he thought it needful to guard the evangelical sayings of the Saviour, both those which counsel against using two coats or sandals, and those against being worn down by anxieties for the time to come. 11. But, employing a zeal beyond his years and persevering in cold and nakedness, and pressing on to the utmost height of poverty, he greatly astonished those about him, grieving countless numbers who prayed to share with him their possessions, on account of the labours they saw him bestowing upon the divine teaching—yet he himself by no means relaxed his austerities. 12. He is said for a good many years to have walked the ground using no sandal whatever, and likewise for very many years to have abstained from the use of wine and of all things beyond his necessary food, so that he fell into danger of overthrowing and ruining his constitution. 13. Affording such examples of a philosophic life to those who beheld him, he naturally roused more of his pupils to a like zeal, so that even of the unbelieving heathen, and those trained in learning and philosophy, not a few were brought under his teaching. These too, genuinely receiving through him in the depth of their souls faith in the divine word, became distinguished at that very season of persecution, so that some of them were taken and perfected by martyrdom.

The first of these, then, was Plutarch, mentioned a little before. As he was being led to death, the man of whom our account speaks, being present with him to the very end of his life, was again all but slain by his fellow-citizens, as having plainly been the cause of his death; but the counsel of God preserved him then also. 2. After Plutarch, the second of Origen's pupils to be shown a martyr was Serenus, who gave proof through fire of the faith he had received. 3. Of the same school the third to be made a martyr was Heraclides, and after him the fourth, Heron—the former still a catechumen, the latter newly baptized—both beheaded. Besides these, of the same school a fifth champion of true religion is proclaimed, another Serenus, who, after the utmost endurance of tortures, is reported to have been punished by beheading. And of the women, Herais, while still a catechumen, received baptism by fire, as he himself somewhere says, and departed this life.

Seventh among these let Basilides be reckoned, who led away the renowned Potamiaena, concerning whom much is still sung even now among the people of the country—how she contended in countless struggles with her lovers for the purity and virginity of her body, in which she excelled (for indeed, besides her soul, the bloom of her body also flowered in its prime), and how, after enduring countless trials, at last, after dreadful tortures fearful to tell, she was perfected by fire together with her mother Marcella. 2. They say that the judge—Aquila was his name—after inflicting cruel torments upon her over her whole body, finally threatened to deliver her to gladiators for the outraging of her body; and she, considering with herself a little while and being asked what her decision was, gave such an answer as seemed to them to utter something impious by their reckoning. 3. No sooner had she received the sentence of condemnation than Basilides, one of those enrolled in the army, took her and led her away to death. As the crowd tried to molest her and to insult her with licentious words, he kept them off, driving away those who insulted her and showing her the utmost pity and humanity. She, accepting the man's sympathy toward her, bade him be of good courage, for she would ask him of her own Lord when she had departed, and would not long after requite him for what he had done toward her. 4. Having said these things she nobly endured her departure, boiling pitch being poured over the various parts of her body, from the soles of her feet up to the crown of her head, slowly and little by little. 5. Such was the contest waged by that maiden worthy of song. Not long after, Basilides, being asked for some reason by his fellow-soldiers to take an oath, affirmed that it was utterly unlawful for him to swear; for he was a Christian, and openly confessed it. At first they thought he was jesting; but when he persisted firmly, he was led to the judge, before whom he confessed his stand, and was committed to bonds. 6. When the brethren in God came to him and inquired the cause of this sudden and strange impulse, he is said to have replied that Potamiaena, three days after her martyrdom, had stood by him at night, placed a crown about his head, and said that she had besought the Lord on his behalf and obtained her request, and that not long after she would take him to herself. Thereupon the brethren imparted to him the seal in the Lord, and on the next day, having distinguished himself by martyrdom for the Lord, he was beheaded. 7. And many others of those at Alexandria are recorded to have come over all at once to the word of Christ in the days mentioned, since Potamiaena appeared to them in their sleep and called them. But let this suffice.

Clement, having succeeded Pantaenus, had charge of the catechizing at Alexandria up to that time, so that Origen too became one of his pupils. Clement, indeed, in composing his treatise of the Stromateis, in the first book set forth a chronological writing, and bounds the times at the death of Commodus; so that it is clear that his studies were laboured under Severus, whose times the present account records.

At this time also another writer, Judas, discoursing in writing on the seventy weeks in Daniel, brings his chronography down to the tenth year of the reign of Severus. He also supposed that the much-talked-of coming of the Antichrist was even then drawing near—so violently had the agitation of the persecution then against us disturbed the minds of the many.

At this time, while Origen was accomplishing the work of catechizing at Alexandria, he did a thing that betokened a mind immature and youthful, yet containing the greatest proof at once of faith and of self-control. 2. For taking the words 'There are eunuchs who have made themselves eunuchs for the kingdom of heaven' in too simple and youthful a sense, and thinking at once to fulfil the Saviour's word, and also—being young in age and conversing on divine things not only with men but with women as well—to shut off from the unbelievers all suspicion of shameful slander, he was moved to carry out the Saviour's word in deed, taking care to escape the notice of most of those about him. 3. But it was not possible for him, though he wished it, to conceal so great a deed. When Demetrius learned of it afterward, as president of the community there, he greatly marvelled at his rashness; yet, approving the eagerness and the genuineness of his faith, he exhorted him to be of good courage, and urged him now the more to cleave to the work of catechizing. 4. Such, then, was he at that time. But not long after, the same Demetrius, seeing him prospering and great and illustrious and renowned among all, fell into something human, and undertook to write to the bishops throughout the world as though the deed were most monstrous—at the time when the most approved and distinguished bishops in Palestine, those of Caesarea and Jerusalem, judging Origen worthy of the office of presbyter and of the highest honour, laid hands on him into the presbyterate. 5. Then, accordingly, when he had advanced to great glory, and acquired a name among all men everywhere and no small renown for virtue and wisdom, Demetrius, having no other ground of accusation, made a grievous slander of the deed long ago done by him as a boy, daring to include in his accusations those who had advanced him to the presbyterate. 6. These things, then, happened a little later. But at that time Origen at Alexandria was accomplishing, without reserve, the work of divine teaching toward all who came to him, night and day, devoting his whole leisure unwearyingly to the divine studies and to those who frequented him. Severus, having held power eighteen years, was succeeded by his son Antoninus. Among those who had played the man in the persecution and after their contests in confession had been preserved by the providence of God was one Alexander, whom we have just shown to be bishop of the church in Jerusalem; having distinguished himself in confessions for Christ, he was deemed worthy of the bishopric there, while Narcissus, who was his predecessor, was still living.

Many other wonderful things the citizens of that community record concerning Narcissus, as from a tradition of the brethren who succeeded one another; among which they relate that such a marvel as the following was wrought through him. 2. Once, during the great vigil of the Pascha, the oil failed the deacons; whereupon, as deep despondency seized the whole multitude, Narcissus ordered those who were preparing the lights to draw water and bring it to him. 3. This being done as soon as said, he prayed over the water and bade them pour it upon the lamps with genuine faith in the Lord; and when they had done this also, beyond all reason, by a marvellous and divine power, its nature was changed from the quality of water into that of oil; and among very many of the brethren there a small portion of it was preserved from that time even to our own day, as a token of the wonder then wrought. 4. Many other things worthy of remembrance they tell concerning the life of this man, among which is this. Certain worthless little men, unable to bear the vigour and firmness of his life, and fearing, from the consciousness of the countless evils they were guilty of, that they might be brought to trial, contrived a plot against him beforehand and stitched together a dreadful slander against him. 5. Then, to assure their hearers, they confirmed the accusations with oaths: the one swore that he might perish by fire, the second that his body might be consumed by a foul disease, the third that he might be blinded in his eyes. But not even so, though they swore, did any of the faithful give heed to them, on account of the temperance and altogether virtuous conduct of Narcissus that shone forth to all. 6. He himself, by no means enduring the wickedness of what was said, and besides having long since embraced the philosophic life, fled from the whole multitude of the church and lived for very many years in deserts and obscure fields. But the great eye of justice did not rest at the things that had been done, 7. and very swiftly pursued the impious men with the very curses by which they had bound themselves in perjury against themselves. The first, from no cause at all, simply when a small spark fell upon the house in which he dwelt, was burnt up at night with his whole household, the whole house being set ablaze. The second was suddenly filled, over his whole body from the soles of his feet to his head, with the very disease he had imprecated upon himself. 8. The third, seeing the issues of the former two and dreading the inescapable justice of the all-seeing God, confessed to all the things they had contrived in common against themselves, and was so worn down with repentance and ceased not from such weeping and tears, until he was destroyed in both his eyes. Such, then, were the punishments these men suffered for their lying.

Narcissus having withdrawn, and it being in no way known where he might be, it seemed good to those who presided over the neighbouring churches to proceed to the ordination of another bishop. Dius was his name; and after he had presided no long time, Germanion succeeded him, and him Gordius; in whose time Narcissus, appearing as it were from a resurrection from somewhere, was again besought by the brethren to take the presidency, all admiring him yet more greatly, both on account of his withdrawal and his philosophy, and above all on account of the vengeance by which God had deemed him worthy.

And since he was no longer able to perform the ministry through his exceeding old age, the dispensation of God called the aforesaid Alexander, who was bishop of another community, to the ministry along with Narcissus, by a revelation that appeared to him at night in a vision. 2. Accordingly, as by some divine intimation, when he had made his journey from the land of the Cappadocians, where he had first been deemed worthy of the bishopric, to Jerusalem, for the sake of prayer and of inquiry into the holy places, those there received him most kindly and would no longer permit him to return home, by another revelation that appeared to them at night and gave a most clear utterance to the most earnest among them. For it disclosed that, going forth outside the gates, they should receive the bishop foreordained for them by God; and having done this, by the common counsel of the bishops who governed the surrounding churches, they constrained him perforce to remain. 3. Alexander himself, indeed, mentions in his own letters to the Antinoites, still preserved among us, his joint presidency with Narcissus, writing thus in these very words at the close of the letter: 'Narcissus salutes you, who held the office of the bishopric here before me, and who is now associated with me by prayers, having completed his hundred and sixteenth year, exhorting you, like myself, to be of one mind.' 4. These things, then, were so. And of the church at Antioch, Serapion having gone to his rest, the bishopric was succeeded by Asclepiades, himself also distinguished in confessions during the persecution. Alexander too mentions his appointment, writing to the Antiochenes thus: 5. 'Alexander, a servant and prisoner of Jesus Christ, to the blessed church of the Antiochenes, greeting in the Lord. Light and easy has the Lord made my bonds, learning during the time of imprisonment that, by the divine providence, Asclepiades, most fit by the worthiness of his faith, has been entrusted with the bishopric of your holy church of the Antiochenes.' 6. He indicates that he sent this letter by Clement, writing thus toward the end: 'These letters, my lords and brethren, I have sent you by Clement the blessed presbyter, a man virtuous and approved, whom you also know and will recognize the better; who, being present here too by the providence and oversight of the Master, has strengthened and increased the church of the Lord.'

Of Serapion's literary labour, it is likely that other memorials too are preserved among others; but to us alone have come down the works To Domnus, who in the time of persecution fell away from faith in Christ to the Jewish will-worship; and those To Pontius and Caricus, men of the Church; and other letters to others; 2. and another discourse composed by him On the so-called Gospel according to Peter, which he wrote in refutation of the things falsely stated in it, on account of certain persons in the community at Rhossus who, on the pretext of the said writing, had turned aside to heterodox teachings. From this it is reasonable to set down a few words, by which he sets forth the opinion he held concerning the book, writing thus: 3. 'For we, brethren, receive both Peter and the other apostles as Christ; but the writings falsely inscribed with their names we, as experienced men, reject, knowing that such things we did not receive. For when I was with you, 4. I supposed that all held to the right faith; and not having gone through the Gospel put forward by them under the name of Peter, I said that, if this is the only thing that seems to bring petty-mindedness among you, let it be read. But now, having learned, from what was told me, that their mind was lurking in some heresy, I will make haste to come to you again; so, brethren, expect me shortly. 5. But we, brethren, having grasped of what heresy Marcian was, who even contradicted himself, not understanding what he said—which you will learn from what has been written to you— 6. for we were able, from others who had practised this very Gospel, that is, from the successors of those who began it, whom we call Docetae (for most of the notions are of their teaching), having borrowed it from them, to go through it and to find that most of it belonged to the right word of the Saviour, but some things were added besides, which we have also appended for you.'

And these are the words of Serapion.
