As for Clement's Stromateis, all eight, they are preserved among us, which he deemed worthy of such a title as this: 'The Stromateis of Gnostic Memoirs according to the True Philosophy, of Titus Flavius Clement.' 2. Equal in number to these are his books entitled Hypotyposeis, in which he mentions Pantaenus by name as his teacher, and sets forth his interpretations of the Scriptures and his traditions. 3. There is also of him a discourse To the Greeks, the Protrepticus; and three books of the work entitled the Paedagogus; and another discourse of his entitled Who is the rich man that is saved; and the treatise On the Pascha; and discussions On fasting and On evil-speaking; and the Exhortation to endurance, or To the newly baptized; and the work entitled the Ecclesiastical Canon, or Against the Judaizers, which he dedicated to Alexander the bishop aforesaid. 4. Now in the Stromateis he has made a tapestry not only of the divine Scripture but also of the writings of the Greeks, if anything seemed to him profitably said by them too; and he mentions the opinions held by many, 5. unfolding both Greek and barbarian teachings, and besides correcting the false opinions of the heresiarchs, and he unfolds much history, furnishing us a subject of much-learned instruction. With all these he mingles also the doctrines of the philosophers, whence fittingly he has made the title of the Stromateis ('Patchworks') suited to his subject. 6. He has used in them also testimonies from the disputed Scriptures: the so-called Wisdom of Solomon, and that of Jesus son of Sirach, and the Epistle to the Hebrews, and those of Barnabas and Clement and Jude; 7. and he mentions the discourse of Tatian To the Greeks, and Cassian, as having himself also composed a chronography; and besides, Philo and Aristobulus, Josephus and Demetrius and Eupolemus, Jewish writers, as all these had shown in writing that Moses and the Jewish race were more ancient than the early origins among the Greeks. 8. And the discourses of the man mentioned are full of much other useful learning; in the first of which he discloses concerning himself that he came very near to the succession of the apostles, and he promises in them also to write commentaries on Genesis. 9. And in his discourse On the Pascha he confesses that he was constrained by his companions to hand down in writing, for those who came after, the traditions he chanced to have heard from the ancient presbyters; and he mentions in it Melito and Irenaeus and certain others, whose accounts also he has set down.

But when he saw that he was not sufficient for the deeper study of divine things, and for the examination and interpretation of the sacred writings, and besides for the catechizing of those who came—who did not allow him even to take breath, one set after another frequenting his school from morning till evening—he divided the multitudes, and choosing out Heraclas from among his acquaintances, a man earnest in divine things and otherwise most learned and not without a share of philosophy, he made him his partner in the catechizing, entrusting to him the first introduction of those just being grounded, and reserving for himself the instruction of those advanced.

So accurate was the examination of the divine words introduced by Origen that he even learned the Hebrew tongue thoroughly, and made the original Scriptures, in the Hebrew letters themselves, current among the Jews, his own possession; and he traced out the editions of the others, besides the Seventy, who had translated the sacred Scriptures, and discovered certain others, differing from the well-worn translations of Aquila, Symmachus, and Theodotion, which he tracked out from some recesses where they had long lain hidden, and brought to light. 2. Concerning these, on account of their obscurity, not knowing whose they might be, he noted only this, that he found the one at Nicopolis near Actium, 3. and the other in another such place. In the Hexapla of the Psalms, after the four well-known editions, he set down not only a fifth, but also a sixth and a seventh translation; and concerning one of these he has again noted that it was found at Jericho in a jar, in the times of Antoninus the son of Severus. 4. All these he brought together into one, and dividing them clause by clause and setting them over against one another, together with the very notation of the Hebrew, he has left us the copies of the so-called Hexapla; arranging separately the edition of Aquila and Symmachus and Theodotion, together with that of the Seventy, in the Tetrapla.

Of these very translators it should be known that Symmachus was an Ebionite. The heresy of the so-called Ebionites is that of those who say that Christ was born of Joseph and Mary, and suppose Him to be a mere man, and insist that the Law must be kept after a more Jewish fashion, as we have learned from the earlier history. And memoirs of Symmachus are still extant, in which he seems, aiming at the Gospel according to Matthew, to establish the aforesaid heresy. These, with other interpretations of the Scriptures by Symmachus, Origen indicates that he received from a certain Juliana, who, he says, received the books in succession from Symmachus himself.

At this time Ambrose too, who held the opinions of the heresy of Valentinus, having been refuted by the truth championed by Origen, and as if illumined in mind by a light, gave his adherence to the doctrine of the Church's orthodoxy. 2. And many others of the learned, as the fame of Origen was noised abroad everywhere, came to him to make trial of the man's competence in the sacred words; and countless heretics, and not a few of the most distinguished philosophers, attended him diligently, being instructed by him not only in divine things but also, almost, in the philosophy of those without. 3. For he introduced as many as he saw of good natural parts to the philosophic studies also, imparting geometry and arithmetic and the other preliminary disciplines, and leading them on to the sects among the philosophers, and expounding their writings, commenting on them and examining each, so that the man was proclaimed a great philosopher even among the Greeks themselves. 4. Many also of the more uncultivated he urged on to the ordinary course of learning, declaring that they would derive from these no small fitness for the contemplation of and preparation for the divine Scriptures; whence especially he reckoned the discipline in the secular and philosophic studies necessary for himself as well.

Witnesses of his attainment in these matters are the Greeks themselves, the philosophers who flourished in his time, in whose writings we have found much mention of the man—now dedicating their own discourses to him, now submitting their own labours to him as to a teacher, for his judgment. 2. What need is there to say these things, when even Porphyry, who settled in our time in Sicily, composing treatises against us and in them attempting to slander the divine Scriptures, and mentioning those who had expounded them, being able to bring no base charge whatever against the doctrines, for lack of arguments turns to reviling, and to slandering the expositors, and most of all Origen? 3. Saying that he had known him in his youth, he attempts to slander him, but unawares rather commends the man—telling the truth in some things, where he could not say otherwise, but lying in others, where he thought he would escape notice; now accusing him as a Christian, now describing his progress in the philosophic studies. 4. Hear, then, what he says in these very words: 'Some, in their eagerness to find a solution—not a renunciation—of the wickedness of the Jewish Scriptures, turned to interpretations incoherent and ill-fitting with the things written, bringing not so much a defence of the foreign matter as approval and praise of their own. For boasting that the things plainly said by Moses are riddles, and divinizing them as oracles full of hidden mysteries, and through their conceit bewitching the critical faculty of the soul, they bring in their interpretations.' 5. Then, after other matters, he says: 'This manner of absurdity is to be traced to a man whom I too, while still quite young, met—a man of great repute, and still in repute through the writings he has left behind, Origen, whose renown is widely spread among the teachers of these doctrines. 6. For this man, having become a hearer of Ammonius, who in our times had made the greatest progress in philosophy, gained much benefit from his teacher in respect of experience in discourse, but in respect of the right choice of life took the opposite road from him. 7. For Ammonius, being a Christian, brought up by Christian parents, when he took to thought and philosophy, straightway changed to the life according to the laws; but Origen, a Greek educated in Greek learning, drove headlong toward the barbarian recklessness; and toward this he carried himself and his attainment in discourse and made merchandise of it—living, as to his manner of life, after the Christian and lawless fashion, but, as to his opinions concerning things and concerning the Deity, playing the Greek and slipping the things of the Greeks under the foreign fables. 8. For he was ever in company with Plato, and was conversant with the writings of Numenius and Cronius, Apollophanes and Longinus and Moderatus and Nicomachus, and of the men of note among the Pythagoreans; and he used also the books of Chaeremon the Stoic and of Cornutus, from whom, having learned the figurative method of the Greek mysteries, he applied it to the Jewish Scriptures.' 9. These things were said by Porphyry in the third treatise of his writings against the Christians, telling the truth concerning the man's discipline and wide learning, but plainly lying (for what would he not do, writing against the Christians?) in those things in which he says that Origen passed over from the Greeks, while Ammonius fell from a life of true religion into the heathen way. 10. For to Origen the teaching of Christ had been preserved from his forefathers, as the earlier history also showed; and to Ammonius the doctrines of divine philosophy remained pure and unimpaired even to the last end of his life, as his very labours testify even now, in the writings he has left, by which he is held in repute among very many—such as that entitled On the Concord of Moses and Jesus, and all the others found among the lovers of the beautiful. 11. Let these things, then, be set forth to establish both the false accusation of the liar and Origen's wide experience in the Greek studies; concerning which, defending himself to certain who blamed him for his zeal in those matters, he writes thus in a certain letter: 12. 'Since I was devoted to the word, and the fame of our competence was going abroad, there came to me now heretics, now those from the Greek studies and especially those in philosophy; it seemed good to me to examine both the doctrines of the heretics and what the philosophers professed to say concerning truth. 13. And this we did, imitating Pantaenus, who before us profited many and had no small preparation in those matters, and Heraclas, who now sits in the presbytery of the Alexandrians, whom I found with the teacher of the philosophic studies, having already persevered with him five years before I began to hear those discourses; 14. and on whose account, having before worn the common dress, he laid it aside and assumed the philosopher's garb, which he keeps to this day, and does not cease to study the books of the Greeks to the best of his power.' 15. And these things were said by him in defence of his Greek discipline. About this time, while he was making his stay at Alexandria, one of the soldiers stood by and delivered letters to Demetrius the bishop of the community and to the then prefect of Egypt, from the governor of Arabia, that they should send Origen with all speed to confer with him. So he came to Arabia; and having quickly brought to its end the object of his coming, he returned again to Alexandria. 16. Some time having intervened, when no small war was kindled in the city, slipping out of Alexandria he went to Palestine and made his stay at Caesarea; where the bishops there requested him to discourse and to interpret the divine Scriptures publicly in the church, although he had not yet received the ordination of the presbyterate. 17. This itself becomes evident from what Alexander the bishop of Jerusalem and Theoctistus of Caesarea, writing about Demetrius, plead somewhat thus: 'He added in his letters that this had never been heard, nor had now happened, that laymen should preach in the presence of bishops'—saying, I know not how, what is plainly not true. 18. For wherever there are found men fit to profit the brethren, they are even invited by the holy bishops to address the people, as at Laranda Euelpis by Neon, and at Iconium Paulinus by Celsus, and at Synnada Theodore by Atticus, our blessed brethren. And it is likely that this happens in other places too without our knowledge.' Thus was the man of whom we speak honoured even while still young, not only by his familiar friends but by bishops of foreign parts. 19. But when Demetrius again recalled him by letters, and urged him by men who were deacons of the church to return to Alexandria, he came back and fulfilled his customary labours.

At this time there flourished many learned men of the Church, whose letters, which they exchanged with one another, it is easy still to find preserved. These too have been kept for us in the library at Aelia, furnished by Alexander who then governed the church there; from which we ourselves have been able to gather together the materials of the subject in hand. 2. Of these, Beryllus has left, besides letters, also various beautiful works; he was bishop of the Arabians at Bostra. Likewise also Hippolytus, who himself too presided over a church somewhere. 3. There has come down to us also a dialogue of Gaius, a most learned man, held at Rome in the time of Zephyrinus against Proclus, who championed the heresy of the Phrygians; in which, curbing the rashness and daring of his opponents in composing new Scriptures, he mentions only thirteen epistles of the holy apostle, not numbering that to the Hebrews with the rest; since indeed even to this day among some of the Romans it is not reckoned to be the apostle's.

But Antoninus, having reigned seven years and six months, was succeeded by Macrinus; and he having lasted a year, again another Antoninus took over the rule of the Romans; in whose first year the bishop of the Romans, Zephyrinus, departed this life, having held the ministry full eighteen years. 2. After him Callistus was entrusted with the bishopric, who, surviving five years, left the ministry to Urban. The emperor Alexander succeeded thereupon to the rule of the Romans, Antoninus having lasted only four years. At this time also, in the church of the Antiochenes, Asclepiades was succeeded by Philetus. 3. The mother of the emperor, Mamaea by name, a woman most devout if ever there was one, since the fame of Origen was noised abroad everywhere, so that it came even to her ears, set great store by being deemed worthy of a sight of the man, and of making trial of his understanding of divine things, admired by all. 4. Being then at Antioch, she summoned him with a military escort. With her he spent some time, and after displaying very many things for the glory of the Lord and for the excellence of the divine teaching, he hastened back to his customary labours.

Then indeed Hippolytus too, composing, among very many other memoirs, the treatise On the Pascha, in which, setting forth a reckoning of times and putting forward a certain canon of a sixteen-year cycle concerning the Pascha, he bounds his times at the first year of the emperor Alexander. Of his other writings, those that have come down to us are these: On the Hexaemeron; On the things after the Hexaemeron; Against Marcion; On the Song; On parts of Ezekiel; On the Pascha; Against all the heresies; and very many others which you may find preserved among many.

From that time also a beginning was made of Origen's commentaries on the divine Scriptures, Ambrose urging him on by countless exhortations—not only by encouragements through words and entreaties, but also by most ungrudging supplies of necessaries. 2. For more than seven shorthand-writers attended him as he dictated, relieving one another at appointed times; and copyists not fewer, together with maidens trained in fair writing. The needful abundant supply of all these Ambrose furnished; nay, more, he brought to him an unspeakable eagerness in the discipline and zeal for the divine oracles, by which especially he urged him on to the composing of commentaries. 3. These things being so, Urban, having held the bishopric of the church of the Romans eight years, was succeeded by Pontian; and that of the Antiochenes, after Philetus, by Zebennus. In their time Origen, 4. a pressing need on account of ecclesiastical affairs requiring him, set out for Greece by way of Palestine, and at Caesarea received the laying-on of hands for the presbyterate from the bishops there. The matters that were thereupon stirred up concerning him, and the things decreed by those who presided over the churches concerning what had been stirred up, and all else that, in his prime, he contributed to the divine word, requiring a treatise of their own, we have recorded with some fullness in the second book of the Apology we have composed on his behalf.

In expounding the first Psalm he has set out a catalogue of the sacred Scriptures of the Old Testament, writing thus in these very words: 'It should not be unknown that the canonical books, as the Hebrews hand them down, are twenty-two, the same in number as the letters among them.' 2. Then, after some matters, he adds, saying: 'These are the twenty-two books according to the Hebrews: that which among us is entitled Genesis, but among the Hebrews, from the beginning of the book, Bresith, which is "In the beginning"; Exodus, Ouellesmoth, which is "These are the names"; Leviticus, Ouikra, "And he called"; Numbers, Ammesphekodeim; Deuteronomy, Elleaddebareim, "These are the words"; Joshua son of Nun, Iosoue ben Noun; Judges, Ruth, among them in one, Sophteim; Kingdoms I and II, among them one, Samuel, "the God-called"; Kingdoms III and IV in one, Ouammelchdavid, which is "the kingdom of David"; Chronicles I and II in one, Dabreiamein, which is "words of days"; Esdras I and II in one, Ezra, which is "helper"; the book of Psalms, Spharthelleim; the Proverbs of Solomon, Meloth; Ecclesiastes, Koelth; the Song of Songs (not, as some suppose, Songs of Songs), Sirassireim; Isaiah, Iessia; Jeremiah with Lamentations and the Epistle in one, Ieremia; Daniel, Daniel; Ezekiel, Iezekiel; Job, Iob; Esther, Esther. And outside these are the Maccabees, which are entitled Sarbethsabanaiel.' 3. These things, then, he sets in the aforesaid treatise. But in the first of those On Matthew, keeping the ecclesiastical canon, he testifies that he knows only four gospels, writing thus: 4. 'As I have learned by tradition concerning the four gospels, which alone are undisputed in the Church of God under heaven: that first was written that according to Matthew, once a tax-gatherer but afterward an apostle of Jesus Christ, who published it for those who came to believe from Judaism, composed in Hebrew letters; 5. second, that according to Mark, who composed it as Peter directed him, and whom Peter also confessed as a son in the catholic epistle, saying in these words: "She who is in Babylon, elect together with you, salutes you, and Mark my son"; 6. and third, that according to Luke, the gospel praised by Paul, made for those from the Gentiles; and after all, that according to John.' 7. And in the fifth of his Expositions of the Gospel according to John the same man says this concerning the epistles of the apostles: 'But he who was made sufficient to become a minister of the new covenant, not of the letter but of the spirit, Paul, who fulfilled the gospel from Jerusalem and round about as far as Illyricum, did not write to all the churches he taught; and to those to whom he wrote, he sent but a few lines. 8. And Peter, on whom the Church of Christ is built, against which the gates of Hades shall not prevail, has left one acknowledged epistle, and let there be also a second; for it is doubted. 9. Why need I speak of him who leaned on the breast of Jesus, John, who has left one gospel, 10. confessing that he could make so many that not even the world could contain them; and who wrote also the Apocalypse, being commanded to keep silence and not write the voices of the seven thunders? He has left also an epistle of very few lines; and let there be also a second and a third, since not all say that these are genuine; but both together are not a hundred lines.' 11. Besides these, concerning the Epistle to the Hebrews, in his Homilies upon it he discusses thus: 'That the character of the diction of the epistle entitled To the Hebrews has not the apostle's vulgarity of speech—he who confessed himself rude in speech, that is, in style—but that the epistle is, in the composition of its diction, more Greek, 12. everyone who knows how to judge differences of style would acknowledge. And again, that the thoughts of the epistle are admirable and not inferior to the acknowledged apostolic writings, this too anyone who attends to the apostolic reading would agree to be true.' 13. To these, after other matters, he adds, saying: 'But I, giving my opinion, would say that the thoughts are the apostle's, but the diction and the composition belong to someone who recorded the apostolic teachings and, as it were, made notes on what was said by the teacher. If, then, any church holds this epistle as Paul's, let it be approved on this score also; for not without reason have the men of old handed it down as Paul's. 14. But who wrote the epistle, the truth God knows; the account that has reached us is, from some who say that Clement, who became bishop of the Romans, wrote the epistle, and from some that it was Luke, who wrote the gospel and the Acts.'

But let this suffice. It was the tenth year of the rule aforesaid when Origen, making his removal from Alexandria to Caesarea, left the catechetical school there to Heraclas. Not long after, Demetrius too, the bishop of the church of the Alexandrians, died, having lasted in the ministry full forty-three years; and Heraclas succeeded him.

At this time Firmilian, bishop of Caesarea of the Cappadocians, was distinguished, displaying such zeal concerning Origen that now he would summon him to the regions about himself for the benefit of the churches, now would set out himself to Judaea and spend some time with him for the sake of advancement in divine things. Moreover, Alexander too, who presided over Jerusalem, and Theoctistus at Caesarea, attending upon him the whole time as upon their only teacher, allowed him to perform the work of interpreting the divine Scriptures and the rest of the ecclesiastical ministry.

Alexander the emperor of the Romans, having completed thirteen years of rule, was succeeded by Maximinus Caesar; who, out of spite against the house of Alexander, which was composed of many believers, raising a persecution, ordered that the rulers of the churches alone should be put to death, as being responsible for the teaching according to the gospel. Then too Origen composed the work On Martyrdom, dedicating the treatise to Ambrose and to Protoctetus, a presbyter of the community at Caesarea, since both had been overtaken by no ordinary distress in the persecution; in which it is recorded that the men distinguished themselves in confession, Maximinus lasting no more than three years. Origen has marked the time of this persecution in the twenty-second book of his Expositions of the Gospel according to John and in various letters.

To Origen at Caesarea, while he was doing his customary work, came many, not only of the people of the country, but also countless pupils from abroad, who had left their native lands. Of these we know as most distinguished Theodore—who was that very Gregory, renowned among the bishops of our day—and his brother Athenodorus; whom, when they were vehemently set upon the Greek and Roman studies, instilling into them a love of philosophy, he urged to exchange their former zeal for the divine discipline. Having spent five whole years with him, they carried away so great an advancement in divine things that, while both were still young, they were deemed worthy of the bishopric of the churches in Pontus.

At this time also Africanus, the writer of the work entitled the Cesti, was known. A letter of his written to Origen is extant, expressing his perplexity, as though the story of Susanna in Daniel were spurious and fabricated; to which Origen replies most fully. 2. Of the same Africanus there have come down to us also other accurately laboured works, five in number, of Chronographies; in which he says that he himself made a journey to Alexandria on account of the great fame of Heraclas, who, as we have shown, having greatly distinguished himself in philosophic discourses and the other Greek studies, was entrusted with the bishopric of the church there. And another letter of the same Africanus is extant, to Aristides, 3. concerning the supposed discrepancy in the genealogies of Christ in Matthew and Luke; in which he most clearly establishes the agreement of the evangelists, from an account that came down to him, which in due course, in the first book of the subject in hand, I have already set forth.

At this time Origen's commentaries on Isaiah, and at the same time those on Ezekiel, were being composed; of which, on the third part of Isaiah, down to the vision of the four-footed beasts in the wilderness, thirty volumes have come down to us, and on Ezekiel twenty-five, which alone he made on the whole prophet. Being then at Athens, he finished those on Ezekiel, 2. and began those on the Song of Songs, and advanced there as far as the fifth treatise; and having returned to Caesarea he brought these too to their end, ten in number. 3. But what need is there at present to make an exact catalogue of the man's works, which would require a leisure of its own? This we have set down in the record of the life of Pamphilus, the holy martyr of our day, in which, showing how great was the zeal of Pamphilus concerning divine things, I set forth the indexes of the library he gathered, both of the works of Origen and of the other ecclesiastical writers; from which whoever pleases may most fully ascertain the works of Origen that have come down to us. But now we must proceed with the sequence of the history.

Beryllus, mentioned a little before, bishop of Bostra in Arabia, perverting the ecclesiastical canon, attempted to bring in certain things foreign to the faith, daring to say that our Saviour and Lord did not pre-exist in a distinct circumscription of being before His sojourn among men, nor had a divinity of His own, but only the Father's dwelling in Him. 2. Concerning this, when very many bishops had held inquiries and discussions with the man, Origen, being invited with others, came down first to a conversation with the man, to test what his mind was; and when he had learned what he asserted, correcting him as not orthodox, and persuading him by reasoning, he set him upon the truth of the doctrine and restored him to his former sound opinion. 3. And there are still extant in writing records both of Beryllus and of the synod held on his account, together with Origen's inquiries with him and the discussions delivered in his community, and all the particulars of what was then done. 4. And countless other things concerning Origen the presbyters of our day hand down in memory, which I think I shall pass over, as not belonging to the present work; but whatever was necessary to know about him may be gathered from the Apology laboured by us, together with the holy martyr of our day, Pamphilus, which we composed with mutual toil for the sake of the captious.

Gordian having completed full six years of the Roman rule, Philip together with his son Philip succeeded to the office. An account holds that he, being a Christian, on the day of the last vigil of the Pascha wished to share in the prayers of the church with the multitude, but was not permitted to enter by him who then presided until he should make confession and enroll himself among those examined as in transgression and holding a place of repentance; for otherwise, had he not done this, on account of the many charges concerning him, he would never have been received by him. And he is said to have obeyed readily, showing by deeds the genuine and reverent disposition of his fear toward God.
It was the third year of his reign when Heraclas, having departed this life after sixteen years of presiding over the churches at Alexandria, was succeeded in the bishopric by Dionysius.

Then indeed, as was natural, the faith increasing and our word being spoken with boldness before all, they say that Origen, being more than sixty years old, since by his long preparation he had now gathered the greatest competence, permitted his public discourses to be taken down by shorthand-writers, a thing he had never before allowed to be done. 2. At this time he composed the eight treatises in answer to the work entitled, against us, The True Word, of Celsus the Epicurean; and the twenty-five volumes on the Gospel according to Matthew, and those on the twelve prophets, of which we have found only twenty-five. 3. There is extant of him also a letter to the emperor Philip himself, and another to his wife Severa, and various others to various persons; of which, as many as we have been able to gather, preserved here and there among different people, we have arranged in separate collections of volumes, that they might no longer be scattered—they exceed the number of a hundred. 4. He writes also to Fabian the bishop at Rome, and to very many other rulers of churches, concerning his orthodoxy. You have the proofs of these too in the sixth book of the Apology written by us concerning the man.

Again, others in Arabia about the time mentioned sprang up as introducers of a doctrine alien to the truth, who said that the human soul, for the present, at the time of death dies together with the bodies and is destroyed with them, but again at the time of the resurrection will come to life with them. And when, accordingly, no small synod had been convened, Origen was again invited; and there too, having raised discussions publicly concerning the question, he carried himself in such a way that the minds of those formerly in error were changed.

Then too another perversion took its beginning, the so-called heresy of the Helkesaites, which was extinguished as soon as it began. Origen mentions it, preaching publicly on the eighty-second Psalm, saying somewhat thus: 'There has come at present a man priding himself greatly on being able to champion an opinion godless and most impious, called that of the Helkesaites, lately risen up against the churches. What evils that opinion speaks I will set before you, that you be not carried away. It sets aside certain parts of every Scripture; it uses again sayings from every Scripture, both of the Old and of the gospel; the apostle it sets aside altogether. It says that to deny is a matter of indifference, and that the man who has understanding will, in necessities, deny with his mouth but not with his heart. And they bring forward a certain book, which they say fell from heaven, and that he who has heard it and believes will receive remission of sins—another remission than that which Christ Jesus granted.'

But Philip, having reigned seven years, was succeeded by Decius; who, out of enmity toward Philip, raised a persecution against the churches, in which Fabian was perfected by martyrdom at Rome, and Cornelius succeeded to the bishopric. 2. In Palestine, Alexander the bishop of the church of Jerusalem, again for Christ standing before the governor's tribunals at Caesarea and distinguishing himself in a second confession, underwent imprisonment, crowned with sleek old age and venerable grey hairs. 3. He, after his splendid and conspicuous testimony at the governor's tribunals, fell asleep in prison, and Mazabanes was appointed his successor in the bishopric at Jerusalem. 4. And in like manner with Alexander, Babylas at Antioch, after confession, having departed this life in prison, Fabius presided over the church there. 5. Now what things, and how great, befell Origen in the persecution, and with what end he met—when the evil demon, matching himself against the man, arrayed his whole host against him and assailed him with every device and power, and beyond all who were warred against at that time bore down upon him with peculiar fury—what and how great things the man endured for the word of Christ: bonds and bodily torments, punishments under iron and in the recesses of the prison; and how for very many days, with his feet stretched four spaces apart in the stocks of torture, he bore threats of fire and all else inflicted by his enemies; and what end his case had, the judge contending with all his might that he should by no means be put to death; and what utterances, full of profit to those needing relief, he left behind afterward—all this very many letters of the man contain, with truth and exactness alike.

The things concerning Dionysius I will set forth from his letter to Germanus, where, telling about himself, he relates thus: 'But I speak before God too, and He knows whether I lie: not on my own counsel, nor without God, did I make my flight; but even before, when the persecution under Decius had been proclaimed, 2. Sabinus that very hour sent a frumentarius to search me out; and I remained four days at my house, awaiting the coming of the frumentarius; but he went all about searching, the roads, the rivers, the fields, where he supposed me to be hidden or walking, but was held by a kind of blindness, not finding the house; for he did not believe that I, being pursued, remained at home. 3. And hardly, after the fourth day, God bidding me remove and marvellously making a way, I and my servants and many of the brethren went out together. And that this was a work of God's providence the sequel showed, in which perhaps we proved useful to some.' 4. Then, after saying something in between, he discloses the things that befell him after his flight, adding this: 'For I, about sunset, together with those with me, was seized by the soldiers and led to Taposiris; but Timothy, by the providence of God, chanced not to be present and was not taken; coming later he found the house deserted and servants guarding it, and us carried off into slavery.' 5. And after other matters he says: 'And what was the manner of His marvellous dispensation? For the truth shall be told. One of the country-folk met Timothy as he fled, distraught, and asked the cause of his haste; and he told the truth, and the man, hearing it 6. (he was going off to feast at a wedding, for it is their custom in such gatherings to spend the whole night), went in and told those reclining at table; and they, with one impulse, as if by signal, all rose up, and rushing swiftly came with all speed, and falling upon us raised a shout; and the soldiers guarding us at once taking flight, they stood over us as we lay on the uncovered pallets. And I— 7. God knows that at first I thought them robbers come for plunder and pillage—remaining on my bed, was naked in my linen garment, and held out the rest of my clothing lying beside me; but they bade me rise and go out as quickly as possible. 8. And then, understanding why they were there, I cried out, beseeching and entreating them to depart and let us be; and if they wished to do any good thing, I asked them to anticipate those who were leading me away and to cut off my head. And as I cried out such things, as those who shared all things with me and were partakers know, they raised me up by force. And I let myself fall flat upon the ground, but they, seizing my hands and feet, dragged me out; and there followed me the witnesses of all these things, Gaius, Faustus, Peter, Paul; 9. who, taking me up, carried me out of the little town, and setting me on a bare ass led me away.' These things Dionysius concerning himself.

The same man, in his letter to Fabius bishop of the Antiochenes, relates thus the contests of those who suffered martyrdom at Alexandria under Decius: 'The persecution among us did not begin with the imperial edict, but anticipated it by a whole year; and the prophet and author of evils to this city, whoever he was, getting the start, moved and incited against us the multitudes of the heathen, kindling them up to their native superstition. Stirred up by him and seizing upon all license for unhallowed deeds, 2. they reckoned this the only piety, the worship of their demons, to thirst for our blood. First, then, seizing an old man, Metras by name, and bidding him utter godless words, 3. when he would not obey, beating his body with clubs and stabbing his face and eyes with sharp reeds, they led him to the suburb and stoned him. 4. Then, leading a faithful woman, Quinta by name, to the idol-temple, they tried to force her to worship; and when she turned away and abhorred it, they bound her by the feet and dragged her through the whole city over the rough pavement, dashing her against the millstones, and at the same time scourging her, and led her to the same place and stoned her. 5. Then with one accord all rushed upon the houses of the godly, and falling upon those whom each recognized as neighbours, they led them off, plundered and pillaged, appropriating the more precious of the treasures, but the cheaper, and whatever was made of wood, scattering and burning in the roads, so that they presented the sight of a city taken by enemies. 6. But the brethren gave way and withdrew, and like those to whom Paul bore witness they received the plundering of their goods with joy; and I know not whether any—unless perhaps some one who fell in their way—up to this point denied the Lord. 7. But also the most admirable virgin then, the aged Apollonia, they seized, and knocking out all her teeth they smote her jaws; and heaping up a pyre before the city they threatened to burn her alive, unless she would utter along with them the proclamations of impiety. She, asking a little respite and being released, leapt vehemently into the fire and was consumed. 8. And seizing Serapion at his own hearth, racking him with cruel tortures and breaking all his joints, they threw him down headlong from the upper story. And no way, no highway, no lane was passable for us, neither by night nor by day, all and everywhere always crying out that, unless one should chant the blasphemous words, he must straightway be dragged off and burnt. And these things flourished in this fashion for a long time; 9. but when sedition and civil war succeeded upon the wretches, it turned their cruelty against us upon one another; and we breathed again a little, as they had no leisure for their wrath against us. But immediately the change from that more merciful reign was announced to us, and great was the fear of the threat hanging over us. 10. And indeed the edict was at hand, almost that very thing foretold by our Lord—the most fearful thing, so as, if possible, to offend even the elect. 11. Howbeit, all cowered; and many of the more distinguished at once, some came forward from fear, others, holding public office, were led on by their duties, others were dragged by those about them; and being called by name they approached the impure and unholy sacrifices, some pale and trembling, as though they were not to sacrifice but themselves to be the victims and offerings to the idols, so that the great crowd standing round mocked them, and it was plain that they were cowards toward everything alike, both toward dying and toward sacrificing; 12. but others ran more readily to the altars, asserting by their boldness that they had not even been Christians before—concerning whom the Lord's prediction is most true, that they shall hardly be saved. Of the rest, some followed one or other of these, and some fled; 13. and some were taken, and of these some went as far as bonds and prison, and some, having been shut up many days, then, even before coming to the tribunal, forswore the faith, and some, having endured tortures up to a point, gave up at the next stage. 14. But the firm and blessed pillars of the Lord, strengthened by Him and receiving power and endurance worthy of and proportionate to the strong faith within them, became admirable martyrs of His kingdom; 15. of whom the first was Julian, a man so gouty that he could neither stand nor walk, brought forward with two others who carried him; of whom the one straightway denied, but the other, Cronion by name, surnamed Eunus, and the old man Julian himself, having confessed the Lord, were carried through the whole city, which is very great, as you know, mounted on camels and scourged aloft, and at last, with all the people pouring round, were consumed with quicklime. 16. And a soldier who stood by them as they were led away and opposed those who insulted them, when they cried out, the most manful man-at-arms of God, Besas, being brought forward and having borne himself bravely in the great war for true religion, was beheaded. 17. And another, a Libyan by race, and by name as well as by blessing truly Macar ('Blessed'), though much exhorted by the judge to deny, would not be induced, and was burnt alive. And after them Epimachus and Alexander, after the long time they remained in bonds, having borne countless agonies, scrapers and scourges, these too were consumed with unquenched fire. 18. And with them four women: Ammonarion, a holy virgin, whom the judge tortured very contentiously for a very long time, since she had declared beforehand that she would utter nothing of what he commanded, having made good her declaration, was led away; and the rest, the most venerable aged Mercuria, and Dionysia, who was the mother of many children but did not love her children above the Lord—the governor, ashamed to torture them further to no purpose and to be worsted by women, put them to death by the sword, taking no further trial of tortures; for their champion Ammonarion had received them on behalf of them all. 19. And Heron and Ater and Isidore, Egyptians, and with them a lad of about fifteen, Dioscorus, were delivered up; and first the youth, the judge attempting to deceive him with words as easily led astray, and to constrain him with tortures as easily yielding, Dioscorus neither was persuaded nor gave way. 20. The rest, having most savagely scraped, when they endured, he gave to the fire also; but Dioscorus, who had shone forth in public and answered most wisely to his questions, he marvelled at and released, saying that he granted him a respite for repentance on account of his age; and now the most godly Dioscorus is with us, having remained for a longer and more enduring contest and prize. 21. And one Nemesion, he too an Egyptian, was first falsely accused of consorting with robbers; but having cleared himself of this most alien slander before the centurion, being informed against as a Christian he came as a prisoner before the governor; and the most unjust man, having mangled him with double the tortures and scourges given to the robbers, burnt him between the robbers, the blessed man being honoured by the example of Christ. 22. And a whole band of soldiers—Ammon and Zeno and Ptolemaeus and Ingenuus, and with them the old man Theophilus—stood before the tribunal; and when one being judged as a Christian was already inclining to denial, these standing by gnashed their teeth, and made signs with their faces and stretched out their hands and gestured with their bodies. 23. And when all turned toward them, before any could lay hold of them, anticipating, they ran up to the bar, declaring themselves Christians, so that the governor and his assessors were terrified, and those being judged appeared most courageous in respect of what they should suffer, while the judges trembled. And these went forth from the tribunals in triumph and exulted in their testimony, God leading them gloriously in triumph.'

And very many others throughout the cities and villages were torn in pieces by the heathen, of whom for the sake of one example I will make mention. Ischyrion was steward to one of the magistrates for hire. His employer ordered him to sacrifice; and when he would not obey, abused him; when he persisted, reviled him; and when he stood firm, taking a very great staff and thrusting it through his bowels and entrails, slew him. 2. What need is there to tell the multitude of those who wandered in deserts and mountains and were destroyed by hunger and thirst and cold and sicknesses and robbers and wild beasts? Of whom the survivors are witnesses of their election and victory; but one deed of these too I will set forth in proof. 3. Chaeremon, exceedingly aged, was bishop of the city called Nilus. He fled to the Arabian mountain with his consort, and did not return; nor could the brethren see them any more, though they searched much, neither themselves nor their bodies. 4. And many on that same Arabian mountain were carried off into slavery by barbarian Saracens; of whom some were hardly ransomed at great cost, and some not even to this day. And these things I have related not in vain, brother, but that you may know how many and how grievous things befell us; of which those who have had more experience would know more.' 5. Then, after a little, he adds, saying: 'These very divine martyrs among us, who now are assessors of Christ and partakers of His kingdom and sharers of His judgment and judges together with Him, received certain of the fallen brethren who had become liable to the charges of sacrificing; and seeing their conversion and repentance, and judging it able to be acceptable to Him who in no wise wills the death of the sinner but rather his repentance, they received and gathered and presented them, and shared with them in prayers and feasts. What, then, brethren, do you counsel us concerning these? 6. What must we do? Shall we stand of one vote and one mind with them, and keep their judgment and grace, and deal kindly with those who have been pitied by them? Or shall we make their judgment unjust, and set ourselves up as judges of their opinion, and grieve kindness, and overturn the order?' These things Dionysius reasonably set down, stirring up the question concerning those who had failed at the time of the persecution.

Inasmuch as Novatus, a presbyter of the church of the Romans, lifted up with pride against these, as though there were no longer any hope of salvation for them, not even if they should perform all things tending to a genuine conversion and pure confession, became the head of a peculiar heresy of those who, in the pride of their reckoning, declared themselves 'the Pure'; 2. on which account a very great synod was convened at Rome, of sixty bishops in number, and of yet more presbyters and deacons, while separately throughout the rest of the provinces the pastors in their several regions deliberated concerning what should be done, a decree was passed by all: that Novatus, together with those who were lifted up with him, and those who chose to consent to the brother-hating and most inhuman opinion of the man, should be held as aliens from the Church; but that the brethren who had fallen into the calamity should be healed and tended with the medicines of repentance. 3. There came to us, then, letters of Cornelius bishop of the Romans to Fabius of the church of the Antiochenes, setting forth the things concerning the Roman synod and what was decided by those in Italy and Africa and the regions there; and again others, composed in the Latin tongue, of Cyprian and those with him in Africa, by which it was made clear that they too agreed that those who had been tried should obtain succour, and that it was reasonable to make the head of the heresy, and all alike who were carried away with him, excommunicate from the catholic Church. 4. With these was joined another letter of Cornelius concerning the things approved at the synod, and again another concerning the things done by Novatus; from which there is nothing to hinder our setting down portions, that those here who read this writing may know the things concerning him. Instructing Fabius, then, what manner of man Novatus was, 5. Cornelius writes these very things: 'But that you may know that this admirable man was long ago aiming at the bishopric, and concealing within himself this his rash desire, using as a cover for his madness the fact that at the first he had the confessors with him, I wish to tell you. 6. Maximus a presbyter of ours, and Urban, who twice reaped the most excellent glory of confession, and Sidonius, and Celerinus, a man who through the mercy of God bore all tortures most steadfastly and by the strength of his faith strengthened the weakness of the flesh and mightily conquered the adversary—these men, then, perceiving him and detecting the craft and duplicity in him, and his perjuries and falsehoods, and his unsociableness and wolf-friendship, returned to the holy Church, and in the presence of many bishops and presbyters and very many laymen declared all his contrivances and villainies, which he had long harboured within himself and kept hid, lamenting and repenting that, persuaded by the crafty and malicious beast, they had for a little while left the Church.' 7. Then, after a little, he says: 'How great a change and reversal, beloved brother, we beheld in a short time wrought upon him! For that most illustrious man, who by certain fearful oaths pledged that he in no wise aimed at the bishopric, suddenly appears as a bishop, flung into the midst as it were by some sleight-of-hand. 8. For this very doctrinaire, this champion of ecclesiastical learning, when he was attempting to wrest and snatch the bishopric not given him from above, chose for himself two associates, men who had despaired of their own salvation, that he might send them to some small and least part of Italy and thence by some fabricated device deceive three bishops, rude and most simple men, affirming and insisting that they must come quickly to Rome, in order that, forsooth, whatever dissension had arisen might be dissolved together with other bishops and by their mediation; 9. and when these had come—being, as we said before, men too simple for the contrivances and knaveries of the wicked—being shut up by certain disordered men like himself, at the tenth hour, drunken and reeling, he forced them by violence, with a kind of feigned and empty laying-on of hands, to give him a bishopric which he claims by ambush and knavery, though it did not belong to him; of whom one not long after returned to the Church, 10. lamenting and confessing his sin, with whom we communicated as a layman, all the people present interceding for him; and to the other bishops we ordained and sent successors into the places where they were. 11. This avenger of the gospel, then, did not know that there must be one bishop in a catholic church, in which—as he was not ignorant, how could he be?—there are forty-six presbyters, seven deacons, seven subdeacons, forty-two acolytes, exorcists and readers together with doorkeepers fifty-two, widows with afflicted persons above fifteen hundred, all of whom the grace and loving-kindness of the Master nourishes; 12. whom neither this great multitude, so necessary in the Church, a number rich and abounding by the providence of God, together with a very great and innumerable people, recalled and turned back from such desperation and renunciation into the Church.' 13. And again, after other matters, he adds these: 'Come, let us next say by what works or what conduct he took courage to lay claim to the bishopric. Was it because from the first he had been conversant in the Church, and had contended many contests on its behalf, and had been in many and great perils for the sake of true religion? 14. Nay, it is not so; to whom the occasion of believing was Satan, who entered into him and dwelt in him a long time; who, being helped by the exorcists, fell into a grievous sickness, and being thought all but certain to die, received, on the very bed where he lay, baptism by affusion—if indeed one should say that such a man received it. Nor yet did he obtain the rest of the things, when he had escaped the sickness, 15. of which he ought to partake according to the canon of the Church, and the being sealed by the bishop; and not having obtained these, how could he have obtained the Holy Spirit?' 16. And again, after a little, he says: 'He who, through cowardice and love of life, at the time of the persecution denied that he was a presbyter. For being asked and exhorted by the deacons that, coming forth from the little chamber in which he had shut himself up, he should help the brethren so far as was lawful and possible for a presbyter to help endangered brethren in need of succour, he was so far from obeying the deacons who exhorted him, that he went off angry and departed; for he said that he no longer wished to be a presbyter, being a lover of another philosophy.' 17. Passing over a few things, he adds these again: 'For this illustrious man forsook the Church of God, in which, having believed, he was deemed worthy of the presbyterate by the grace of the bishop who laid hands on him for the order of the presbyterate; who, being hindered by all the clergy, and also by many laymen, since it was not lawful that one baptized by affusion in bed through sickness, as this man was, should enter into any order, asked that he might be permitted to ordain this one only.' 18. Then he adds another, the worst of the man's enormities, saying: 'For when he has made the offerings and is distributing to each his portion and delivering it, he compels the wretched men, instead of blessing, to swear, holding the hands of him who receives with both his own and not letting go until they say this on oath (for I will use his own words): "By the blood and the body of our Lord Jesus Christ never to leave him and turn to Cornelius." 19. And the wretched man does not taste until he has first cursed himself, and instead of saying the Amen as he receives that bread, he says, "I will not return to Cornelius."' 20. And after other matters he says these things again: 'But know now that he has been stripped and made desolate, the brethren leaving him day by day and returning to the Church; whom also Moses, the blessed martyr, who lately among us bore a noble and admirable testimony, while still in the world, perceiving his audacity and madness, made him excommunicate, together with the five presbyters who with him had separated themselves from the Church.' 21. And at the close of the letter he has made a catalogue of the bishops who came to Rome and condemned the folly of Novatus, noting together both their names and the community over which each presided; and of those who did not come to Rome, 22. but agreed by letters with the vote of the aforesaid, he mentions the names together with the cities from which each wrote. These things, then, Cornelius wrote to set forth to Fabius bishop of Antioch.

To this same Fabius, who was inclining somewhat toward the schism, Dionysius of Alexandria also wrote, and discussing many other things concerning repentance in his letters to him, and going through the contests of those who had lately then suffered martyrdom at Alexandria, relates, among the rest of his history, a thing full of wonder, which it is necessary to hand down here in this writing, being as follows: 2. 'But this one example, which befell among us, I will set forth for you. There was among us a certain Serapion, a faithful old man, who had lived blamelessly the greater part of his time, but in the trial had fallen. This man often besought, and no one heeded him; for indeed he had sacrificed. Falling sick, he continued three successive days speechless and senseless, 3. but recovering a little on the fourth, he called his daughter's son and said, "How long, child, do you hold me back? I beseech you, make haste, and quickly release me; call me one of the presbyters." 4. And having said this, he was again speechless. The boy ran to the presbyter; but it was night, and he too was sick. He could not come; but, since an injunction had been given by me that those departing this life, if they besought it—and especially if they had also entreated it before—should be released, that they might depart in good hope, he gave the lad a little of the Eucharist, bidding him soak it and drop it into the old man's mouth. 5. The boy returned bringing it; and when he had come near, before he entered, Serapion again reviving said, "Are you come, child? The presbyter could not come, but do you quickly what was commanded, and release me." The boy soaked it, and at the same time poured it into his mouth; and when he had swallowed a little, he straightway gave up the spirit. 6. Was he not plainly preserved and remained until he could be loosed, and, his sin being blotted out, could be acknowledged on account of the many good deeds he had done?'

These things Dionysius. But let us see what manner of things he also wrote to Novatus, who was then troubling the brotherhood of the Romans. Since, then, he made certain of the brethren a pretext of his apostasy and schism, as having been forced by them to come to this, see in what manner he writes to him: 'Dionysius to Novatian his brother, greeting. If, as you say, you were led against your will, you will show it by withdrawing of your own will. For one ought to suffer anything whatever rather than rend the Church of God; and the martyrdom for the sake of not making a schism was not less glorious than that for the sake of not worshipping idols—nay, in my judgment even greater. For there a man bears witness for his own single soul, but here for the whole Church. And now, if you should persuade or constrain the brethren to come to concord, your achievement will be greater than your fault, and the one will not be reckoned, but the other will be praised. But if, when they will not obey, you are unable, save by all means your own soul. I pray that you may fare well, holding to peace in the Lord.'

These things also to Novatus. He writes also to those in Egypt a letter concerning repentance, in which he has set forth his opinions concerning the lapsed, describing the grades of transgressions. And to Colon (this man was bishop of the community of the Hermopolitans) 2. there is extant a writing of his own concerning repentance, and another, hortatory, to his flock at Alexandria. Among these is also that written to Origen concerning martyrdom; and to the brethren at Laodicea, over whom Thelymidres was bishop, and likewise to those in Armenia, over whom Meruzanes was bishop, he writes concerning repentance. 3. Besides all these, he writes also to Cornelius at Rome, having received from him the letter against Novatus; in which he signifies, disclosing that he had been invited by Helenus the bishop of Tarsus in Cilicia, and the rest with him, Firmilian of Cappadocia, and Theoctistus of Palestine, to meet at the synod at Antioch, where certain were attempting to strengthen the schism of Novatus. 4. Besides these, he writes that it had been announced to him that Fabius had fallen asleep, and that Demetrian had been appointed his successor in the bishopric of Antioch; and he writes also concerning the one at Jerusalem in these very words: 'For the admirable Alexander, being in prison, blessedly fell asleep.' 5. Next after this there is extant also another letter of Dionysius to those at Rome, a diaconal one, through Hippolytus; and to the same he sets forth another concerning peace, and likewise concerning repentance; and again another to the confessors there, who still held with the opinion of Novatus; and to these same two more, after they had come over to the Church, he writes. And conversing likewise by letters with very many others, he has left manifold benefits to those who even now show zeal concerning his writings.

The Seventh Book of the Ecclesiastical History contains the following: I. On the malignity of Decius and Gallus. II. The bishops of the Romans in their time. III. How Cyprian, with the bishops of his province, first laid down that those turning from heretical error must be purified by washing. IV. How many letters Dionysius composed on this matter. V. On the peace after the persecution. VI. On the heresy of Sabellius. VII. On the all-defiling error of the heretics, and the God-sent vision of Dionysius, and the ecclesiastical canon he received. VIII. On the heterodoxy of Novatus. IX. On the godless baptism of the heretics. X. On Valerian and the persecution under him. XI. On the things that befell Dionysius and those in Egypt at that time. XII. On those who suffered martyrdom at Caesarea in Palestine. XIII. On the peace under Gallienus. XIV. The bishops who flourished at that time. XV. How Marinus suffered martyrdom at Caesarea. XVI. The story concerning Astyrius. XVII. On the signs at Paneas of the mighty work of our Saviour. XVIII. On the throne of James. XIX. On the festal letters of Dionysius, where he also gives a canon concerning the Pascha. XX. On the things that befell at Alexandria. XXI. On the pestilence that fell upon it. XXII. On the reign of Gallienus. XXIII. On Nepos and the schism connected with him. XXIV. On the Apocalypse of John. XXV. On the letters of Dionysius. XXVI. On Paul of Samosata and the heresy formed by him at Antioch. XXVII. On the distinguished bishops known at that time. XXVIII. How Paul, being refuted, was excommunicated. XXIX. On the heterodox perversion of the Manichaeans, then just beginning. XXX. On the ecclesiastical men distinguished in our own day, and which of them continued up to the siege of the churches.

The seventh book of the Ecclesiastical History the great Dionysius, bishop of the Alexandrians, will again help us to compose in his own words, relating in turn each of the things done in his time through the letters he has left; and from this point my account will make its beginning.

Decius, having held power not a full two years' time, was straightway slaughtered together with his sons, and Gallus succeeded him. At this time Origen died, having completed seventy years all but one. Dionysius, indeed, writing to Hermammon, says this concerning Gallus: 'But Gallus neither understood the evil of Decius nor foresaw what it was that had tripped him up; he stumbled against the same stone that lay before his eyes. For when his reign was prospering and affairs were going according to his mind, he drove out the holy men who were interceding with God for his peace and welfare; and so, together with them, he persecuted also the prayers offered on his behalf.'

So much concerning him. But in the city of the Romans, Cornelius having completed the bishopric about three years, Lucius was appointed his successor; and he, having ministered not a full eight months, at his death handed on the office to Stephen. To him Dionysius addressed the first of his letters concerning baptism, no small question having then been stirred up, whether those turning from any heresy whatsoever ought to be purified by washing; for an ancient custom had prevailed of using, in such cases, only the prayer with laying-on of hands.

First of the men of that time, Cyprian, pastor of the community at Carthage, held that they ought not to be received unless they had first been purified from their error by washing. But Stephen, thinking that nothing should be innovated contrary to the tradition that had prevailed from the beginning, was greatly displeased at this.

Dionysius, therefore, having conferred with him very fully on this matter by letters, at the end discloses that, the persecution having abated, the churches everywhere, having turned away from the innovation of Novatus, had resumed peace among themselves. He writes thus:

'Know now, brother, that all the churches throughout the East, and still farther off, that were formerly divided, are united, and all the presidents everywhere are of one mind, rejoicing exceedingly at the peace that has come beyond expectation: Demetrian at Antioch, Theoctistus at Caesarea, Mazabanes at Aelia, Marinus at Tyre (Alexander having fallen asleep), Heliodorus at Laodicea (Thelymidres being at rest), Helenus at Tarsus and all the churches of Cilicia, Firmilian and all Cappadocia. For I have named only the more conspicuous of the bishops, that I may neither attach length to the letter nor weight to the discourse. 2. But all the Syrias and Arabia, which you succour from time to time and to which you have now written, and Mesopotamia and Pontus and Bithynia, and, in a word, all everywhere rejoice in the concord and brotherly love, glorifying God.' 3. These things Dionysius. But Stephen, having completed the ministry two years, was succeeded by Xystus. To him Dionysius wrote a second letter concerning baptism, in which he discloses at once the opinion and judgment of Stephen and of the other bishops, saying this concerning Stephen: 4. 'He had written before concerning Helenus and Firmilian and all those from Cilicia and Cappadocia and clearly Galatia and all the neighbouring nations in succession, that he would not communicate with them either, for this same cause—because, he says, they rebaptize the heretics. 5. And consider the magnitude of the matter. For truly decrees concerning this have been passed in the greatest synods of the bishops, as I learn, so that those who come over from heresies are first catechized, then washed and purified afresh from the filth of the old and unclean leaven. And concerning all these things I wrote, entreating him.' 6. And after other matters he says: 'And to our beloved fellow-presbyters also, Dionysius and Philemon, who formerly agreed with Stephen and wrote to me on the same matters, I wrote before briefly, and now also at greater length.' But so much concerning the question mentioned.

Signifying in the same place concerning the heretics of Sabellius, as prevalent in his time, he says this: 'For concerning the doctrine now stirred up at Ptolemais of the Pentapolis, which is impious and holds much blasphemy concerning the Almighty God the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, and much unbelief concerning His only-begotten Son, the firstborn of all creation, the Word made man, and an insensibility concerning the Holy Spirit—when there came to me from both sides both documents and the brethren who were to discuss it, I wrote certain things, as I was able, God granting it, expounding the matter in a more instructive manner; copies of which I have sent you.'

And in the third of those concerning baptism, which the same Dionysius writes to Philemon the presbyter at Rome, he sets down these things: 'But I also read the treatises and traditions of the heretics, defiling my soul for a little while with their all-abominable notions, yet getting from them this benefit, that I refuted them in my own mind and abhorred them far more. 2. And indeed, when a certain brother of the presbyters tried to restrain me and feared lest I should be soiled by the mire of their wickedness—for it would harm my own soul, and he spoke truly, as I perceived—a vision sent from God came to me and strengthened me, 3. and a voice that came to me commanded, saying expressly: "Read everything that may come into your hands; for you are competent to set right and to test each thing, and this was from the beginning the cause of your faith." I accepted the vision as agreeing with the apostolic saying, addressed to the stronger: "Be approved money-changers."' 4. Then, after saying something about all the heresies, he adds, saying: 'This rule and pattern I received from our blessed pope Heraclas. For those coming from the heresies, although they had departed from the Church—or rather had not even departed, but, while seeming to assemble with us, were informed against as frequenting some teacher of false doctrine—he drove from the Church, and when they besought him did not receive them, until they had publicly declared all that they had heard among their opponents; and then he gathered them, not needing for them another baptism, for they had previously received the holy baptism from him.' 5. And again, after exercising the problem at length, he adds these: 'I have learned this too, that it was not now only that those in Africa introduced this, but long ago, in the time of the bishops before us, in the most populous churches and in the synods of the brethren, at Iconium and Synnada and among many, it was so decided; whose counsels I cannot bear to overturn and to cast them into strife and contention. For "you shall not remove," he says, "the landmarks of your neighbour which your fathers set."' 6. The fourth of his letters concerning baptism was written to Dionysius at Rome, who had then been deemed worthy of the presbyterate, but not long after received also the bishopric there; from which it is possible to learn how this man too, learned and admirable, was attested by Dionysius of Alexandria. He writes to him, after other matters, mentioning the affairs of Novatus, in these words:

'For we reasonably hate Novatian, who rent the Church and drew certain of the brethren into impieties and blasphemies, and brought in a most unholy teaching concerning God, and slanders our most gracious Lord Jesus Christ as merciless; and besides all these, sets aside the holy washing, and overturns the faith and confession that precede it, and altogether banishes the Holy Spirit from them, even if there were any hope that He would remain with or return to them.'

And his fifth was written to Xystus the bishop of the Romans; in which, after saying much against the heretics, he sets forth a thing of this kind that had happened in his time, saying: 'For indeed, brother, I need counsel and ask your opinion, a certain matter having come to me, fearing lest I be in error. 2. For one of the brethren who assemble, reckoned faithful, of old standing, and before my ordination—I think also before the appointment of the blessed Heraclas—having shared in the assembly, and being present at the recent baptism of some, and hearing the questions and answers, came to me weeping and lamenting himself and falling at my feet, confessing and disavowing the baptism with which he had been baptized among the heretics, that it was not this nor had any communion at all with this, for it had been filled with impiety and blasphemies; 3. and saying that his soul was now utterly pricked, and that he had no boldness to lift up his eyes to God, setting out from those unholy words and deeds, and on this account beseeching to obtain this most pure purification and reception and grace. 4. Which I did not dare to do, saying that his long communion was sufficient for this. For one who had heard the Eucharist and joined in saying the Amen, and stood at the table and stretched out his hands for the reception of the holy food, and received it, and partaken of the body and blood of our Lord a long time, I would not dare to build up anew from the beginning. But I bade him take courage and approach the participation of the holy things with firm faith and good hope. 5. But he ceases not to mourn, and shudders to approach the table, and scarcely, when exhorted, endures to be present at the prayers.' 6. Besides the aforesaid, there is also another letter of the same man concerning baptism, addressed by him and the community over which he presided to Xystus and the church at Rome, in which by a lengthy demonstration he prolongs the discourse on the underlying question. And another of his after these is extant, to Dionysius at Rome, that concerning Lucian. And concerning these matters, so much.

But concerning the persecution under him, which raged most violently, what things the same man, with others, underwent for his piety toward the God of all, his own words will show, which he sets down thus, in answer to Germanus, one of the bishops of his time who attempted to speak ill of him: 2. 'I am in danger of falling into great folly and senselessness indeed, being brought to the necessity of relating the wonderful dispensation of God toward us. But since, he says, "it is good to hide the secret of a king, but glorious to reveal the works of God," I will come to grips with the violence of Germanus. 3. I came before Aemilianus, not alone, but there followed me my fellow-presbyter Maximus and the deacons Faustus, Eusebius, and Chaeremon, and one of the brethren from Rome who was present came in with us. 4. Aemilianus did not at the outset say to me, "Do not assemble." For that was superfluous to him, and a last consideration, since he was running back to the first; for his word was not about our not assembling others, but about our not even being Christians ourselves, and from this he commanded me to cease, thinking that, if I changed, the rest would follow me. 5. But I answered not unfittingly, nor far from the saying, "We must obey God rather than men"; but openly testified that I worship the one God who alone is, and no other, nor would I change nor ever cease being a Christian. Thereupon he ordered us to depart to a village near the desert, called Cephro. 6. But hear the very words spoken by both, as they were recorded. When Dionysius and Faustus and Maximus and Marcellus and Chaeremon had been brought in, Aemilianus, the deputy-governor, said: "I have discoursed with you orally too concerning the kindness which our lords have shown toward you; 7. for they have given you the power of safety, if you are willing to turn to that which is according to nature and to worship the gods who preserve their empire, and to forget those that are against nature. What, then, say you to these things? For I do not expect that you will be ungrateful for their kindness, since they exhort you to the better." 8. Dionysius answered: "Not all worship all gods, but each certain ones, whom they reckon such. We, therefore, worship and adore the one God and Maker of all things, who also entrusted the empire to the most God-beloved Augusti, Valerian and Gallienus; and to Him we pray continually for their empire, that it may abide unshaken." 9. Aemilianus, the deputy-governor, said to them: "And who hinders you from worshipping this one also, if he is a god, together with the natural gods? For you were ordered to worship gods, and gods whom all know." Dionysius answered: "We worship no other." 10. Aemilianus, the deputy-governor, said to them: "I see that you are at once ungrateful and insensible of the clemency of our Augusti; wherefore you shall not be in this city, but shall be sent to the parts of Libya, to a place called Cephro; for this place I have chosen by the command of our Augusti. And it shall by no means be permitted either to you or to any others to hold assemblies or to enter the so-called cemeteries. But if anyone shall appear either not to have gone to this place which I have commanded, or shall be found in any assembly, 11. he will bring the peril upon himself; for the needful vigilance shall not be wanting. Depart, then, whither you have been ordered." And though I was sick, he hurried me off, granting not a single day's respite. What leisure, then, had I left for assembling or not assembling?' 12. Then, after other matters, he says: 'But neither did we withdraw from the perceptible assembly with the Lord; but those in the city I gathered more diligently, as though present—absent in body, as he said, but present in spirit—and at Cephro a large church sojourned with us, some of the brethren following from the city, others coming together from Egypt. And there too God opened to us a door for the word. 13. And at first we were persecuted, we were stoned; but afterward not a few of the heathen, leaving the idols, turned to God; for then for the first time the word was sown among them through us, who had not before received it, 14. and as if for this purpose God had led us away to them, when we had fulfilled this ministry He led us away again. For Aemilianus wished to remove us to rougher and more Libyan places, as it seemed, and commanded all to stream together from every quarter into the Mareotis, assigning villages throughout the region to each, but stationed us rather in the road and to be the first taken. For he was clearly arranging and preparing that, whenever he wished to seize us, he might have all easy to take. And when I had been commanded to go to Cephro, 15. I did not know where in the world this place was, having scarcely even heard the name before; and yet I went off cheerfully and undisturbed. But when it was announced to me that I should remove to the parts of Colluthion, those present know how I was affected (for here I will accuse myself): 16. at first I was vexed and exceedingly displeased; for although the places happened to be more familiar and more accustomed to us, yet they said that the district was bare of brethren and earnest men, and exposed to the molestations of travellers and the inroads of robbers; 17. but I found comfort when the brethren reminded me that it was nearer to the city, and that, while Cephro brought us much intercourse with brethren from Egypt, so that we could hold a wider assembly, there—the city being nearer—we should more continually enjoy the sight of those truly beloved and most dear and dearest; for they would come and rest, and, as in suburbs lying farther off, there would be assemblies in turn. And so it was.' 18. And after other matters concerning the things that befell him, he again writes thus: 'Germanus indeed prides himself on his many confessions; he has much to say of things that have happened against himself: as many sentences as he can count concerning us, confiscations, proscriptions, plunderings of goods, losses of dignities, contempt of worldly glory, scorn of the praises of governors and councillors and of the contrary, threats and outcries and perils and persecutions and wandering and straitness and the endurance of manifold affliction—such as befell me under Decius and Sabinus, such as down to now under Aemilianus. 19. But where did Germanus appear? What account is there of him? But I forbear the great folly into which I am falling because of Germanus, on which account I leave the detailed narration of what has happened to the brethren who know it to tell.' 20. The same man also, in his letter to Domitius and Didymus, again mentions the events of the persecution in these words: 'But our own people, being many and unknown to you, it is superfluous to enumerate by name; only know that men and women, both young and old, both maidens and aged women, both soldiers and private persons, every race and every age, some by scourges and fire, some by the sword, having conquered the contest, have received the crowns. 21. But for some not even a very long time sufficed to appear acceptable to the Lord, as it seems also not for me up to now; wherefore He who says, "In an acceptable time I heard you, and in a day of salvation I helped you," has reserved me for what time He himself knows to be fitting. 22.
