But one might marvel also at those of them who suffered martyrdom in their own land, where countless numbers, men together with women and children, despising the transitory life for the teaching of our Saviour, endured diverse deaths: some of them, after scrapings and rackings and most grievous scourgings and countless other manifold tortures dreadful to hear, were given over to fire; some were swallowed up in the sea; others courageously stretched out their own heads to those who cut them off; some died under the tortures; others perished by famine; and others again were crucified, some after the manner customary for malefactors, and some yet more cruelly, nailed head downward, and kept alive until they perished by famine upon the very crosses.

And since we said that Phileas was a man of much account also for the learning of those without, let him come forward as his own witness, at once to show what manner of man he was, and to relate the martyrdoms that befell at Alexandria in his time more exactly than we, in these words: 2. From the writings of Phileas to the Thmuites: 'All these examples and patterns and noble tokens being set before us in the divine and sacred Scriptures, the blessed martyrs with us, without delay, fixing the eye of the soul purely upon the God over all, and taking into mind the death for the sake of true religion, held fast to their calling; finding our Lord Jesus Christ to have become man for us, that He might cut off all sin and lay up for us provisions for the entrance into eternal life. For "He counted it not a thing to be grasped to be equal with God, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, and being found in fashion as a man, humbled himself unto death, even the death of the cross." 3. Wherefore also the Christ-bearing martyrs, emulating the greater gifts, endured every toil and every contrivance of torments, not once only, but some even a second time; and though the bodyguards vied against them in all manner of threats, not only in words but also in deeds, they did not yield in resolve, because perfect love casts out fear. 4. To recount whose virtue and the courage shown under each torture, what account would suffice? For, license being given to all who wished to insult them, some struck with clubs, others with rods, others with scourges, others again with thongs, and others with cords. 5. And the spectacle of the maltreatments was a varied one and held much wickedness in it. For some, with their two hands bound behind, were hung up on the wood and stretched in every limb by certain machines; then thus, throughout the whole body, the torturers, by command, applied themselves—not, as with murderers, on the sides only, but also on the belly and legs and cheeks they punished with the instruments; others were hung suspended from the portico by one hand, having from the joints and limbs a tension more dreadful than every pain; others were bound facing the pillars, not standing on their feet, but with the bonds drawn tight by the weight of their bodies forcing them down. 6. And this they endured not only while the governor conversed with them and was at leisure, but well-nigh through the whole day. For when he passed on to others, he left those in charge of his authority to keep watch over the former, if perchance any, overcome by the tortures, seemed to be giving way; and he ordered them mercilessly to apply the bonds, and afterward, when they were at their last gasp, to lay them down and drag them on the ground; 7. for there was not even a part of any thought for us among them, but they so thought and acted as though we were no longer existing, the adversaries having devised this second torture, besides the blows. 8. There were also those who, after the maltreatments, lay upon the wood, both feet stretched apart through the four holes, so that of necessity they lay upon their backs upon the wood, unable to stand because of the fresh wounds from the blows over the whole body; and others, flung upon the ground, lay there from the combined assault of the tortures, presenting to the beholders a sight more dreadful than the act, bearing on their bodies the manifold and various devices of the tortures. 9. These things being so, some died under the tortures, putting the adversary to shame by their endurance; some, shut up half-dead in the prison, after not many days, worn out by the pains, were perfected; and the rest, obtaining recovery by tending, with time and the stay in prison grew more confident. 10. Thus, then, when it was ordered that the choice should lie open, either, by touching the accursed sacrifice, to be unmolested and to obtain from them the accursed freedom, or, by not sacrificing, to receive the sentence of death, without delay they went gladly to death; for they knew the things foreordained for us by the holy Scriptures. For it says, "He who sacrifices to other gods shall be utterly destroyed," and that "You shall have no other gods but me."' 11. Such are the words of the martyr who was truly both a philosopher and a lover of God, which, before the final sentence, while still in the prisoners' ranks, he had sent to the brethren of his community, at once setting forth the things in which he was, and at the same time urging them on to hold fast, even after him, to the true religion in Christ for which he was on the point of being perfected. 12. But what need is there to say much, and to set forth new contests after new of the godly martyrs throughout the world, especially of those no longer besieged by common law, but in the manner of war?

Already, indeed, soldiers, surrounding in a circle a whole little town of Christians in Phrygia, every soul of it, and setting fire to it, burned it up, together with the infants and women who called upon the God over all; because all the inhabitants of the city, with one accord—the curator himself and the generals, with all in office and the whole people—confessing themselves Christians, would in no way obey those who commanded idolatry. 2. And another man who had attained Roman dignity, Adauctus by name, of a family distinguished among the Italians, a man who had advanced through every honour with the emperors, so that he had blamelessly passed through the general administrations of what is among them called the magistracy and the office of catholicus, distinguished in all these things by his achievements in true religion and his confessions of the Christ of God, was adorned with the diadem of martyrdom, enduring the contest for true religion in the very office of catholicus.

Why need I now mention the rest by name, or count the multitude of the men, or depict the manifold maltreatments of the wonderful martyrs—now slain with axes, as happened to those in Arabia; now having their legs broken, as befell those in Cappadocia; sometimes hung up on high by the feet, head downward, and, a slow fire being kindled beneath, suffocated by the smoke given off from the burning fuel, as was inflicted on those in Mesopotamia; sometimes having their noses and ears and hands cut off and the rest of their members and parts butchered, as was the case at Alexandria? 2. Why need I rekindle the memory of those at Antioch, roasted on gridirons of fire, not to death, but for a prolonged punishment; and others who plunged their right hands into the very fire sooner than touch the accursed sacrifice? Some of whom, fleeing the trial, before they were taken and came into the hands of the plotters, threw themselves down from on high from lofty houses, accounting death a prize snatched from the wickedness of the impious. 3. And a certain holy and wonderful one in the virtue of her soul, but in body a woman, and otherwise renowned among all at Antioch for wealth and birth and good repute, who had brought up by the laws of true religion a pair of daughters distinguished for the bloom and prime of their bodies—when the great envy stirred against them, searching out by every means where they lay hid, busied itself about them, and then, learning that they were staying in a foreign land, deliberately summoned them to Antioch, and they were now caught within the soldiers' nets—seeing herself and her daughters in straits, and setting before them in words the dreadful things to come from men, and the most unbearable of all dreadful things, the threat of fornication, and exhorting that neither she nor her daughters should endure to hear of it even with the tips of their ears, and saying that to betray their souls to the slavery of the demons was worse than all deaths and than every destruction, suggested that the one release from all these things was flight to the Lord. 4. And then, having together agreed in resolve, and decently arranging their bodies with their garments, when they had come to the very middle of the road, asking the guards for a little space to withdraw, they flung themselves into a river flowing by. 5. These, then, destroyed themselves. But another pair of virgins at Antioch itself, in all things godly and truly sisters, illustrious in family, splendid in life, young in years, fair in body, reverent in soul, pious in manner, wonderful in zeal—as though the earth could not bear to carry such as these—the worshippers of the demons commanded to be cast into the sea. 6. Such things, then, befell among these. But others in Pontus suffered things dreadful to the ears: pierced in the fingers, through the tips of the nails, with sharp reeds in both hands; and others, lead being melted by fire, having the seething and red-hot material poured over their backs, and roasted in the most necessary parts of the body; 7. and others endured, through their secret members and entrails, shameful and unfeeling sufferings, not even to be told in words, which the noble and lawful judges, displaying their cleverness as if it were some excellence of wisdom, more ambitiously devised, ever striving to surpass one another with newly found maltreatments, as if for the prizes of a contest. 8. And the last of the calamities was when, at length, wearied by the excess of evils and worn out with killing, and having had their fill and surfeit of the shedding of blood, they turned to what they reckoned kind and humane, so as to seem no longer to contrive anything dreadful against us; 9. for they said it was not fitting to defile the cities with the blood of fellow-citizens, nor to charge the supreme rule of the rulers with cruelty, since it was gracious and mild toward all, but rather that the benefit of the humane and imperial power should be extended to all, no longer punishing them with death; for this punishment against us had been remitted, on account of the humanity of the rulers. 10. Then it was commanded that the eyes should be gouged out and one of the two legs maimed. For these were to them the humane things and the lightest of the punishments against us, so that already, on account of this humanity of the impious, it is no longer possible to tell the multitude beyond all account of those who first had their right eyes cut out with the sword and then these cauterized with fire, and their left feet again made useless at the joints by branding-irons; and after these things were condemned to the copper mines throughout the province, not so much for service as for ill-usage and hardship; and besides all these, of others who fell into other contests, which it is not possible even to recount (for their deeds of valour surpass all account). 11. In these things, having shone forth throughout the whole world, the magnificent martyrs of Christ naturally astounded the eyewitnesses of their courage everywhere, and presented in themselves manifest proofs of the truly divine and unspeakable power of our Saviour. To mention each by name would be long, not to say impossible.

Of the rulers of the church who suffered martyrdom in the notable cities, let the first proclaimed by us, on the monuments of the godly, as a martyr of the kingdom of Christ, be Anthimus, the bishop of the city of the Nicomedians, who was beheaded; 2. and of the martyrs at Antioch, the best in his whole life, a presbyter of the community there, Lucian, who at Nicomedia, the emperor himself being present, proclaimed the heavenly kingdom of Christ, first by an apology in word, then also in deeds. 3. Of the martyrs in Phoenicia the most distinguished would be the in all things God-beloved pastors of the rational flocks of Christ: Tyrannion, bishop of the church at Tyre, and Zenobius, a presbyter of that at Sidon, and besides Silvanus, bishop of the churches about Emesa. 4. But this last, becoming food for wild beasts with others at Emesa itself, was taken up into the choirs of martyrs; and the two at Antioch glorified the word of God by their endurance unto death—the one, the bishop, being given over to the depths of the sea, and the other, Zenobius, the best of physicians, dying bravely under the tortures applied to his sides. 5. Of the martyrs in Palestine, Silvanus, bishop of the churches about Gaza, was beheaded at the copper mines in Phaeno, together with others, thirty-nine in number all but one; and there the Egyptian bishops Peleus and Nilus, with others, endured death by fire. 6. And let the great glory of the community of Caesarea be mentioned by us among these—Pamphilus, a presbyter, the most admirable of those of our day, the excellence of whose deeds of valour we shall record at the proper time. 7. And of those at Alexandria, and throughout all Egypt and the Thebaid, who were illustriously perfected, let Peter, bishop of Alexandria itself, be recorded first, a divine ornament of the teachers of the true religion in Christ; and of the presbyters with him, Faustus and Dius and Ammonius, perfect martyrs of Christ; and Phileas and Hesychius and Pachymius and Theodore, bishops of the churches about Egypt; and besides these, countless others distinguished, who are remembered by the communities of their country and place; whose contests, who throughout the whole world contended for the true religion toward the Deity, and to relate exactly each of the things that befell them, it is not for us to hand down in writing, but it would be proper to those who took in the matters by sight. Those, however, at whose deeds I myself was present, I will make known also to those after us by another writing. 8. But in the present account I will add to what has been said the recantation of the things wrought against us, and the things that befell from the beginning of the persecution, being most useful to those who shall read. 9. Now, as for the affairs of the Roman government before the war against us, in what times the conduct of the rulers was friendly and peaceful toward us, of how great an abundance of good things and of prosperity it was deemed worthy, what account could suffice to relate? when those who most held the supreme rule, having completed their tenth and twentieth years, passed their time in festivals and solemn assemblies and most radiant banquets and rejoicings, with all settled peace. 10. And while their power thus grew unimpeded and advanced to greatness day by day, suddenly, changing their peace toward us, they raised a truceless war; nor was the second year of such a movement yet fulfilled, when something new, happening with respect to the whole empire, overturned all affairs. 11. For an unfavourable sickness having fallen upon the chief of those mentioned, by which his mind too was now brought to derangement, together with him who after him had been honoured with the second place, he resumed the common and private life; and these things had not yet been so done, when the whole empire was divided into two parts—a thing handed down to memory as never before having happened at any former time. 12. And after no very long interval, the emperor Constantius, having conducted his whole life most gently and most kindly toward his subjects and most affectionately toward the divine word, leaving behind a legitimate son, Constantine, as emperor and Augustus in his stead, by the common law of nature ended his life, and was first proclaimed among them as one of the gods, having been deemed worthy after death of all honour such as might be owed to an emperor, the most gracious and gentle of emperors; 13. who indeed alone of those of our day passed the whole time of his rule worthily of his sovereignty, and in other respects showed himself most gracious and beneficent toward all, and in no way took part in the war against us, but kept the godly under him unharmed and unmolested, and neither pulled down the houses of the churches nor devised anything else against us, and so received a happy and thrice-blessed end of life, alone in his reign dying graciously and gloriously, with a legitimate son as successor, most prudent and most pious in all things. 14. His son Constantine, immediately from the outset proclaimed a most perfect emperor and Augustus by the armies, and long before these by God himself, the King of all, set himself up as an emulator of his father's piety toward our word. Such was he; and Licinius after these things was declared, by the common vote of the rulers, emperor and Augustus. 15. These things grievously vexed Maximinus, who was still up to that time styled only Caesar above all the rest; who, being most especially tyrannical, snatching the dignity for himself, was Augustus, having made himself so by himself. Meanwhile he who, as we have shown, after his abdication had resumed power, being detected in plotting death against Constantine, ended his life by a most shameful death; and his honorary inscriptions and statues and all such things as are customarily set up, as those of an unholy and most impious man, were the first to be thrown down.

His son Maxentius, who set up the tyranny at Rome, at the beginning feigned our faith, to please and flatter the people of the Romans, and on this account ordered his subjects to relax the persecution against the Christians, putting on a show of piety, that he might appear gracious and much more mild than his predecessors; 2. but he did not prove in deeds such as he was hoped to be, but, running aground upon all unholy deeds, left undone no work of defilement and licentiousness, committing adulteries and all manner of corruptions. Indeed, separating from their husbands their lawful wives, and insulting them most shamefully, he sent them back again to their husbands; and these things he practised, attempting them not against obscure or undistinguished persons, but most of all insulting the most eminent of those who had attained the first places of the Roman senate. 3. All cowered before him—peoples and rulers, both renowned and obscure—and were worn down by the dread tyranny; and even when they kept quiet and bore the bitter slavery, there was nevertheless no deliverance from the murderous cruelty of the tyrant. On some small pretext, indeed, he once gave the people over to slaughter by his bodyguards, and countless multitudes of the Roman people were slain in the midst of the city, not by Scythians nor barbarians, but by the spears and full armour of their own people; 4. and the number of senators slain for the sake of plotting against their property it is not even possible to reckon, countless being put to death now on one feigned pretext, now on another. 5. And the crown of the tyrant's evils drove him to sorcery, now, by magic devices, cutting open pregnant women, now searching the entrails of newborn babes, and slaughtering lions, and composing certain unspeakable rites for the summoning of demons and the averting of the war; for through these he had every hope that victory would be achieved for him. 6. This man, then, playing the tyrant at Rome, it is not even possible to say what things he did in enslaving his subjects, so that they came to be in extreme scarcity and want even of the necessary food, such as at Rome those of our day do not remember to have happened at any other time. 7. And the tyrant in the East, Maximinus, secretly making a friendly compact with him at Rome, as toward a brother in wickedness, took care for a very long time to escape notice; but being detected later, he paid the deserved penalty. 8. And it was a marvel how this man too carried off prizes akin and brotherly—nay, rather the first prizes and the victory—of the wickedness of the tyrant at Rome. For the foremost of the wizards and magicians were deemed worthy of the highest honour with him, since he was most timid and most superstitious, and set great store by the error concerning the idols and the demons; indeed, without divinations and oracles, he was not able, so to speak, to venture to move so much as a fingernail's breadth; 9. for which reason he attacked the persecution against us more violently and more persistently than those before him, commanding that temples be raised in every city and that the precincts long demolished by lapse of time be zealously renewed, and appointing priests of idols in every place and city, and over these, for each province, a high priest, some one of those most conspicuous in public life, who had distinguished himself through every public service, with a troop of soldiers and a bodyguard; and lavishly granting to all charlatans, as to pious men and dear to the gods, governorships and the greatest privileges. 10. Proceeding from these things, he vexed and oppressed, not one city nor one country, but whole provinces utterly under him, with exactions of gold and silver and untold sums of money, and with most grievous impositions and various other condemnations. Indeed, taking away from the wealthy the substance acquired from their ancestors, he bestowed riches in heaps and piles of money all at once upon the flatterers about him. 11. And to such a pitch of drunken excess and intoxication was he carried, that in his cups he was deranged and beside himself, and gave such orders in his drunkenness as, when he had become sober the next day, brought him to repentance; and leaving to none any superlative in surfeiting and profligacy, he set himself up as a teacher of wickedness to the rulers and the ruled about him, leading the army to grow soft through all luxury and licentiousness, and inciting governors and commanders to proceed against the subjects by plunderings and rapacities, all but joining with him in tyranny. Why need I mention the man's passionate and shameful deeds, or count up the multitude of those he debauched? 12. Indeed, he could not pass by a city without having in every case wrought the corruption of women and the snatching away of virgins. 13. And in these things he succeeded against all—not only against the Christians; who, despising death, set his great tyranny at naught. For the men, having endured fire and iron and nailings and wild beasts and the depths of the sea and the cutting off of limbs and brandings and the piercing and gouging out of eyes and the maiming of the whole body, and besides these famine and mines and bonds, showed in all things endurance for the sake of true religion rather than exchanged the worship due to God for idols; 14. and the women again, no less than the men, made manly by the teaching of the divine word, some, undergoing the same contests as the men, carried off equal prizes of virtue; and others, when dragged off for corruption, gave up their souls to death sooner than their bodies to corruption. 15. Indeed, alone of those debauched by the tyrant, a Christian woman, most distinguished and illustrious of those at Alexandria, by a most manly resolve overcame the passionate and licentious soul of Maximinus, renowned otherwise for wealth and birth and learning, yet setting all in the second place to chastity; whom, though he greatly importuned, he was not able to put to death, ready as she was to die, his desire prevailing over his rage rather, but punishing her with exile he took away all her substance. 16. And countless others, by the rulers in the provinces, unable even to hear the threat of fornication, endured every kind of tortures and rackings and death-bearing punishment. Wonderful, then, were these too; but exceedingly the most wonderful was the woman at Rome, truly the most noble and most chaste of all those whom the tyrant there, Maxentius, doing the like to Maximinus, attempted to debauch. 17. For when she learned that those who served the tyrant in such matters had come to her house (and she too was a Christian), and that her husband—and that too a prefect of the Romans—from fear had given them leave to take and lead her away, she asked for a brief space, as though to adorn her body, and went into her chamber, and being alone drove a sword into herself, and dying straightway, left her corpse to the procurers, but by her very deeds, more eloquent than any voice, declared to all men, both those now living and those who should come after, that the virtue among Christians is alone unconquerable and indestructible by riches. 18. So great a tide of wickedness was wrought together at one and the same time by the two tyrants who had divided between them the East and the West; and who, searching out the cause of so many evils, would doubt to declare it to be the persecution against us? especially since the great confusion did not cease before the Christians recovered their freedom of speech.

Throughout the whole ten years' time of the persecution there was no respite for them from plotting and warring against one another. The sea was unnavigable, nor was it possible for any to sail in from any quarter without being subjected to all manner of maltreatments, racked and torn in their sides and examined with tortures of every kind, lest perchance they came from the enemies on the other side, and at last brought to crosses or to the punishment by fire. 2. Besides these, preparations of shields and breastplates, and makings ready of arrows and spears and the rest of the warlike array, and of triremes and naval armaments, were being put together in every place; nor was there anything for anyone to expect but the onset of wars on every day. And to these the famine and pestilence afterward fell upon them, concerning which we shall relate what is needful at the proper time.

Such were the things that extended throughout the whole persecution, which in the tenth year, by the grace of God, wholly ceased, having begun to abate after the eighth year. For when the divine and heavenly grace showed its visitation toward us to be gracious and merciful, then indeed even our rulers—those very men through whom of old the wars against us were waged—most marvellously changing their minds, sang a recantation, quenching by gracious proclamations and most gentle edicts concerning us the fire of the persecution kindled to so great a height. 2. But it was not any human cause that was the occasion of this, nor any pity, as one might say, or humanity of the rulers—far from it; for more and more grievous things were devised against us by them daily, from the beginning and up to that time, with manifold devices ever newly contriving maltreatments against us in various ways; but it was the manifest visitation of the divine providence itself, being reconciled to its own people, but proceeding against the author of the evils and venting its wrath upon the chief instigator of the wickedness of the whole persecution. 3. For even if these things had to come about by divine judgment, yet 'woe,' says the word, 'to him through whom the offence comes.' A God-sent punishment, therefore, overtook him, beginning from his very flesh and proceeding to his soul. 4. For suddenly an abscess formed about the middle of his secret parts, then a deep fistulous ulcer, and an incurable eating away of these into his innermost entrails; from which an indescribable multitude of worms swarmed and a death-bearing stench breathed forth, since the whole bulk of his body, from his gluttony, had even before the sickness been changed into an excess of fat, which, then rotting, presented to those who approached an unbearable and most horrible sight. 5. Of the physicians, therefore, some, not being able to endure at all the surpassing foulness of the stench, were slaughtered; and others, when the whole swollen mass had fallen into a state past hope of recovery and they could give no help, were mercilessly put to death.

But the author of the writing, after such a confession, immediately, and not long after, being released from his pains, departed life. This man, an account holds, was the chief cause of the calamity of the persecution, having, long before the movement of the rest of the emperors, forced the Christians in the army, and first of all those in his own household, to turn aside, and having removed some from their military rank and most shamefully insulted others, and already even threatened others with death, and at last stirred up his colleagues in the empire to the persecution against all; of whom it is not fitting to pass over in silence the end of life that befell themselves. 2. Four, then, having divided the rule over all; of whom those preeminent in time and honour, having lasted not even two full years after the persecution, were removed from the empire, as has been shown by us before, and, having passed the remaining time of their life in a common and private manner, met such an end of life as follows: 3. the one who had been deemed worthy of the first place in honour and in time was worn out by a long and most painful weakness of body, and the one who held the second place after him broke off his life by the noose, suffering this according to a certain demonic foretokening, on account of the very many reckless deeds he had dared. 4. And of those after these, the last, whom indeed we said had become the author of the whole persecution, suffered such things as we have already shown; but the one who preceded him, the most gracious and gentle emperor Constantius, having passed the whole time of his rule worthily of his sovereignty, and in other respects showing himself most gracious and beneficent toward all, and besides keeping aloof from the war against us, and preserving the godly under him unharmed and unmolested, and neither pulling down the houses of the churches nor devising any other new thing at all against us, received a truly happy and thrice-blessed end of life, alone in his reign dying graciously and gloriously, with a legitimate son as successor to the empire, most prudent and most pious in all things; 5. who, immediately from the outset, proclaimed a most perfect emperor and Augustus by the armies, set himself up as an emulator of his father's piety toward our word. Such was the issue of life of the four aforementioned, coming about at differing times. 6. Of these the only one still left, he whom we mentioned a little before, together with those afterward introduced into the rule, made the aforesaid confession manifest to all through the written document set forth above.

The Ninth Book of the Ecclesiastical History contains the following: I. On the feigned relaxation. II. On the perversion that followed. III. On the newly set up idol at Antioch. IV. On the petitions against us. V. On the forged memoirs. VI. On those who suffered martyrdom at this time. VII. On the writing set up against us on pillars. VIII. On the things that befell afterward in famine and pestilence and wars. IX. On the overthrow of the life of the tyrants, and what utterances they used before their end. X. On the victory of the God-beloved emperors. XI. On the final destruction of the enemies of true religion.

The recantation of the imperial command set forth above was published throughout all Asia and in every place, and in the provinces around it. When these things had been accomplished in this manner, Maximinus, the tyrant in the East, most impious if any ever was, and become a most bitter enemy of true religion toward the God of all, being in no way pleased with what had been written, instead of the published letter ordered by word of mouth the rulers under him to relax the war against us. For since it was not lawful for him otherwise to gainsay the judgment of his superiors, putting away the aforesaid law in a corner, and taking care that it should not be brought to light in the parts under him, by an unwritten command he ordered the rulers under him to relax the persecution against us; and they signified the order to one another in writing. 2. At any rate, Sabinus, who among them was honoured with the dignity of most eminent prefect, made known the emperor's mind to the governors of the provinces by a Latin letter, of which the rendering is to this effect: 3. 'With most earnest and devoted zeal the divinity of our masters, the most divine emperors, long ago determined to bring the minds of all men to the holy and right way of life, that even those who seemed to follow a custom alien to the Romans should render the worship due to the immortal gods. 4. But the obstinacy of certain persons and their most harsh resolve came to such a pitch that they could neither be drawn back from their own purpose by the just reasoning of the command, nor be frightened by the impending punishment. 5. Since, therefore, it happened that by such conduct many were bringing themselves into peril, the divinity of our masters, the most powerful emperors, according to the inborn nobility of their piety, judging it foreign to their most divine purpose to bring men into so great a peril from such a cause, has commanded, through my devotedness, to write to your sagacity, that if any of the Christians be found following the worship of his own nation, you should free him from molestation and peril against him, and should reckon that none ought to be punished on this pretext; since by the lapse of so long a time it has been established that they could in no way be persuaded to withdraw from such obstinacy. 6. Your diligence ought, therefore, to write to the curators and the magistrates and the praepositi of the district of each city, that they may know that henceforth it does not behove them to take further thought of this letter.' 7. Thereupon those in the provinces, reckoning the purpose of what was written to them to be genuine, made the imperial mind manifest by letters to curators and magistrates and those set over the country districts. And not only by writing did these things advance among them, but in deeds much sooner; carrying out, as it were, the imperial intent, all whom they held shut up in prisons for their confession of the Deity they brought forth into the open and set free, releasing those of them who had been given over to the mines for punishment; for they supposed, being deceived, that this was in truth the emperor's pleasure. 8. And when these things had been so accomplished, suddenly, like a light shining forth out of a gloomy night, in every city one might see churches gathered together and assemblies thronged with multitudes, and the rites customarily performed in them; and every one of the unbelieving heathen was no little astounded at these things, marvelling at the strangeness of so great a change, and crying out that the God of the Christians was great and alone true. 9. And of our own people, those who had faithfully and manfully contended through the struggle of the persecutions recovered their freedom of speech again toward all; but as many as had become diseased in their faith and were storm-tossed in their souls eagerly hastened to their own healing, beseeching and asking the right hand of salvation from the strong, and entreating God to be gracious to them; 10. and then also the noble champions of true religion, freed from their suffering in the mines, set out for their homes, passing through every city, proud and radiant, full of unspeakable gladness and of a freedom of speech which it is not even possible to interpret in words. 11. Crowds thronging with men accomplished their journey through the midst of the highways and marketplaces, hymning God with songs and psalms; and you might see those who a little before had been driven from their homelands as prisoners under most cruel punishment, recovering their own hearths with cheerful and joyful faces, so that even those who before had thirsted for our blood, seeing the wonder beyond all hope, rejoiced together at what had come to pass.

These things the tyrant, who was a hater of the good and a plotter against all good things, and who, we said, ruled over the parts of the East, could no longer bear, nor did he endure that they should be accomplished in this manner for even six full months. At any rate, contriving everything for the overthrow of the peace, first he attempts on a pretext to bar us from assembly in the cemeteries, then through certain wicked men he sends an embassy against us to himself, having incited the citizens of Antioch to ask of him, as if for a very great favour, that he would in no way permit any of the Christians to dwell in their country; and he contrived that others too should put forward the same. Of all these the chief at Antioch itself was Theotecnus, a clever charlatan and wicked man, alien to his name; he was reputed to be curator of the affairs of the city.

This man, then, having waged very many campaigns against us, and having taken pains in every way to hunt out our people from their hiding-places like some unhallowed thieves, and having contrived everything for slander and accusation against us, and become the cause of death to countless numbers, at last set up a certain idol of Zeus Philios by means of certain juggleries and sorceries, and, devising for it unhallowed rites and ill-omened initiations and accursed purifications, displayed the marvel even to the emperor through oracles, as it seemed. And indeed this man too, by flattery suited to the pleasure of the ruler, roused up the demon against the Christians, and said that the god had commanded that the Christians, as his enemies, be driven beyond the bounds of the city and of the fields about the city.

Having forged, then, Memoirs of Pilate and of our Saviour, full of every blasphemy against Christ, by the resolve of the greater they sent them throughout all the empire under him, charging by proclamation that in every place, both country and city, these be set out openly to all, and that the schoolmasters give them to the children, instead of lessons, to study and to hold in memory. 2. While these things were being accomplished in this manner, another commander, whom the Romans call a duke, at Damascus in Phoenicia, seizing certain disreputable women of ill fame out of the marketplace, and threatening to apply tortures to them, compelled them to say in writing that they had once been Christians, and were privy to lawless deeds among them, and that in the very houses of the Lord they practised licentious things, and whatever else he wished them to say to the slander of the doctrine. And he too, putting their words into memoirs, communicated them to the emperor; and indeed at his command these writings too were published in every place and city.

But this commander, not long after, having become his own slayer by his own hand, paid the penalty of his malignity. As for us, flights were again stirred up, and grievous persecutions, and again dreadful risings of the governors throughout all the provinces against us, so that even some of those distinguished in the divine word, being taken, received the irrevocable sentence of death. Three of these, at Emesa, a city of Phoenicia, having confessed themselves Christians, were given over to be food for wild beasts; among them was a bishop, Silvanus, exceedingly aged, who had completed full forty years of the ministry. 2. At the same time also Peter, who presided most illustriously over the communities at Alexandria, a divine ornament of bishops both for the excellence of his life and for his discipline in the sacred words, seized on no charge, with no expectation having gone before, thus suddenly and unaccountably, as by the command of Maximinus, was beheaded; and with him also several others of the bishops in Egypt underwent the same. 3. And Lucian, a man in all things most excellent, of continent life and trained in the sacred studies, a presbyter of the community at Antioch, being brought to the city of the Nicomedians, where the emperor then chanced to be staying, and having delivered before the ruler his defence of the teaching over which he presided, was committed to prison and put to death. 4. So many things, in a short time, were contrived against us by the good-hating Maximinus, that this persecution seemed to have been roused against us much more grievously than the former.

In the very midst of the cities, a thing which never at any other time, the decrees of the cities against us, and the rescripts of imperial ordinances in answer to these, engraved upon tablets of bronze, were set up; and the children in the schools carried Jesus and Pilate and the memoirs forged for our insult in their mouths every day. 2. Here it seems to me necessary to insert this very writing of Maximinus that was set up on the pillars, that at once the boastful and proud arrogance of the man's hatred of God may be made plain, and the sleepless wickedness-hating of the holy justice that overtook him close upon his heels against the impious; driven on by which, not long after he both took counsel concerning us the contrary, and decreed it by written laws. 3. Copy of the rendering of Maximinus's rescript in answer to the decrees against us, taken from the pillar at Tyre: 'At last the feeble boldness of the human mind has had strength to shake off and scatter all the obscurity and mist of error, which before this besieged the senses—not so much of the impious as of the wretched men—wrapped in the deadly darkness of ignorance, and to recognize that it is governed and established by the good-loving providence of the immortal gods; 4. which thing it is incredible to say how welcome, how most pleasant and dear it has become to us, as a very great proof of your God-loving disposition you have given, since even before this it was unknown to none what manner of observance and piety toward the immortal gods you happened to hold, you with whom is known the faith not of bare and empty words, but of continual and marvellous notable deeds. 5. Wherefore your city might worthily be called a foundation and dwelling-place of the immortal gods. By many examples, at any rate, it appears to flourish through the presence with it of the heavenly gods. 6. Behold, then, your city, neglecting all things that concern its private interests, and overlooking its former prayers for its own affairs, when it perceived again that those of the accursed vanity were beginning to creep abroad, and, like a fire neglected and slumbering, were filling up great conflagrations as the brands rekindled, straightway, without any delay, fled for refuge to our piety, as to a mother-city of all true religions, asking some cure and help; 7. which saving thought it is plain the gods have cast into you for the faith of your piety. That one, therefore, that one, the most high and greatest Zeus, who presides over your most splendid city, who delivers your ancestral gods and wives and children and hearth and homes from all destructive corruption, has breathed into your souls the saving resolve, showing and making plain how excellent and splendid and saving it is to approach, with the worship due, the rites and the holy worship of the immortal gods. 8. For who could be found so foolish or so void of all understanding as not to perceive that it is by the good-loving zeal of the gods that it comes to pass that neither does the earth deny the seeds entrusted to it, baffling the hope of the husbandmen with empty expectation; nor again is the sight of impious war established unhindered upon the earth, and bodies, the temper of heaven being corrupted, dragged down to death in drought; nor is the sea, swelling under the blasts of immoderate winds, heaped into crests; nor do unlooked-for hurricanes, breaking forth, stir up a destructive tempest; nor again does the earth, the nurse and mother of all, sinking down from its lowest depths in fearful trembling, nor do the overlying mountains, when chasms open, fall to ruin—all of which, and things still far more grievous than these, no one is ignorant to have often come to pass before this time? 9. And all these things came about through the destructive error of the empty vanity of those lawless men, when it prevailed upon their souls, and well-nigh, so to speak, oppressed all parts of the world with shameful deeds.' 10. To these things, after others, he adds: 'Let them behold in the broad plains the crops now flourishing and waving with their ears, and the meadows, through good rains, gleaming with growths and flowers, and the temper of the air restored gentle and most mild; 11. let all henceforth rejoice that, through our piety and rites and the honour due, the might of the most powerful and steadfast air has been appeased, and on this account let them, securely and at peace, enjoy and take pleasure in the most serene calm. And as many as, wholly profited, have come back from that blind error and wandering to a right and most excellent mind, let them rejoice the more, as those snatched from an unlooked-for storm or a grievous sickness, and reaping a sweet enjoyment of life for the future; 12. but if they persist in their accursed vanity, let them be separated and driven far away from your city and its territory, as you requested, so that thus, in accordance with your praiseworthy zeal in this matter, your city, being separated from all defilement and impiety, may, with its inborn purpose, obey, with the worship due, the rites of the immortal gods. 13. And that you may know how welcome to us your request in this matter has been, of our own accord, even without decrees and without petition, our soul, most eager for the love of good, grants leave to your devotedness to ask whatever great gift you wish in return for this your God-loving purpose. 14. And now ask to do this and to receive it; for you shall obtain it without any delay; which, being granted to your city, shall furnish for all time a testimony of your God-loving piety toward the immortal gods, and shall show to your sons and descendants that you have obtained worthy rewards from our love of good, for this your choice of life.' 15. Such things against us were set up on pillars throughout every province, shutting off our affairs from all good hope, so far at least as lay in men; so that, according to that very divine oracle, at these things, 'if possible, even the elect themselves' should be 'offended.' 16. And already, indeed, when the expectation among most had all but fainted away, suddenly, while those who served the writing set forth against us were still accomplishing their journey by the road in certain regions, the God who champions His own Church, all but curbing the great vaunting of the tyrant against us, displayed His heavenly alliance on our behalf.

The customary rains and showers, then, the season being wintry, withheld their wonted bounty upon the earth, and an unlooked-for famine fell upon us, and upon this a pestilence, and besides an outbreak of another disease—an ulcer which, from its fiery nature, was fitly called the carbuncle; which, creeping over the whole body, wrought perilous dangers for the sufferers, but most of all, settling especially upon the eyes, made countless numbers of men, together with women and children, blind. 2. In addition to these, the war against the Armenians rose up against the tyrant—men of old both friends and allies of the Romans; whom, being themselves Christians and zealous in their piety toward the Deity, the God-hated man, having attempted to compel to sacrifice to idols and demons, made enemies instead of friends and foes instead of allies. 3. All these things, then, flowing together at one and the same season, confuted the boldness of the tyrant's vaunting against the Deity, since for the sake of his zeal for the idols and his siege against us he had boasted that neither famine nor pestilence nor war had befallen in his times. These things, then, coming on together and at once, contained also the prelude of his overthrow. 4. He himself, accordingly, was being worn down, together with his armies, in the war against the Armenians; and the rest of those who dwelt in the cities under him were grievously wasted at once by the famine and the pestilence, so that two thousand five hundred Attic drachmas were given in exchange for a single measure of wheat. 5. Countless, then, were those dying in the cities, and yet more those in the country and villages, so that the once populous registers of the country folk now nearly suffered complete erasure, well-nigh all being destroyed at once by want of food and by the pestilential disease. 6. Some, then, thought it right to barter away their dearest possessions to the wealthier for the scantiest food; others, selling off their property little by little, were driven to the last extremity of want; and some already, chewing small fragments of hay and recklessly eating certain destructive herbs, ruined and destroyed the constitution of their bodies. 7. And some of the noble women in the cities, driven by want to a shameless necessity, came forth to beg in the marketplaces, displaying a token of their former free-born nurture by the modesty of their faces and the seemliness of their attire. 8. And some, shrivelled up like dead images, here and there at their last gasp, reeling and slipping from inability to stand, fell down, and stretched out prone in the midst of the open streets, besought that a small fragment of bread be held out to them, and, with their soul at its last breaths, cried out that they were hungry, having strength for this most painful word alone; 9. while others, the more well-to-do, astounded at the multitude of those who begged, after giving countless gifts, came at last to a harsh and unfeeling disposition, expecting that they themselves would soon suffer the same as the beggars; so that already, in the midst of the marketplaces and lanes, dead and naked bodies, cast out unburied for many days, presented to the beholders a most pitiable sight. 10. Indeed, some even became food for dogs, on which account chiefly the living turned to the killing of dogs, from fear lest, going mad, they should work the eating of men. 11. And not least did the pestilence too feed upon all houses, but most of all those which the famine, on account of their abundance of food, was not able to wear out; the wealthy, at any rate—rulers and governors and countless of those in office—as if of set purpose left to the pestilential disease by the famine, underwent a swift and most rapid end. All places, then, were full of wailings, and through all the lanes and marketplaces and streets there was nothing else to behold but lamentations, with the flutes and beatings customary with them. 12. In this manner, then, warring with two weapons, those aforesaid of pestilence and famine at once, death devoured whole families in a short time, so that one might see the bodies of two and three dead being borne forth at a single funeral. 13. Such were the wages of the vaunting of Maximinus and of the decrees of the cities against us, when also the tokens of the zeal and piety of the Christians in all things became conspicuous to all the nations. 14. For alone, in so great a crisis of evils, displaying their compassion and humanity by their very deeds, throughout each day some persevered in the tending and burial of the dying (and they were tens of thousands for whom there was none to care), while others gathered together into one assembly the multitude of those throughout the whole city wasted by the famine, and distributed bread to all, so that the matter became noised abroad among all men, and they glorified the God of the Christians, and confessed them, convicted by the very facts, to be truly the only pious and godly. 15. And upon these things being thus accomplished, the great and heavenly Champion of the Christians, God, having displayed His threat and indignation against all men through the things mentioned, in requital for what they had immeasurably shown toward us, restored to us again the gracious and radiant beam of His providence toward us, most marvellously, as in deep darkness, making light to shine forth for us from Himself, and making manifest to all that God Himself had been throughout the overseer of our affairs—now scourging and at the proper time turning back His people through afflictions, and again, after sufficient discipline, showing Himself gracious and kindly to those who set their hopes upon Him.

Thus, then, when Constantine—who, we said before, was an emperor sprung from an emperor, and pious from a most pious and in all things most prudent father—and Licinius after him, both honoured for understanding and piety, had by the King of all and God of the universe and Saviour been roused up against the two most impious tyrants, and arrayed themselves for war by law, with God fighting on their side most marvellously, Maxentius fell at Rome by the hand of Constantine, and the one in the East, surviving him no long time, himself too came to a most shameful end by the hand of Licinius, who was not yet at that time gone mad. 2. But Constantine, who was first both in honour and in rank of the empire, taking pity on those tyrannized over at Rome, and calling upon God the heavenly and His Word, even Jesus Christ Himself the Saviour of all, as his ally through prayers, advanced with his whole army, procuring for the Romans their ancestral freedom. 3. When Maxentius, then, trusting rather to the devices of sorcery than to the goodwill of his subjects, did not dare to advance even so far as the gates of the city, but with a countless multitude of soldiers and innumerable companies of armies had fortified every place and country and city, as many as had been enslaved under him round about Rome and all Italy, the emperor, leaning on the alliance from God, came on and, in the first and second and third array of the tyrant, defeating them most thoroughly, advanced over the greater part of Italy, and was already very close to Rome itself; 4. then, that he might not be compelled to war against the Romans for the tyrant's sake, God Himself, as if by certain bonds, drew the tyrant far away from the gates; and those things long ago recorded against the impious—as if in a tale, distrusted by most, yet trustworthy to the faithful, inscribed in the sacred books—He confirmed by their very plainness, simply speaking, to all, both faithful and unbelieving, who took in the marvels with their eyes. 5. Just as, then, in the time of Moses himself and the ancient godly race of the Hebrews, 'the chariots of Pharaoh and his host He cast into the sea, and his chosen captains were drowned in the Red Sea, the deep covered them,' in the very same manner Maxentius too, and the soldiers and bodyguards about him, 'sank into the depth like a stone,' when, turning his back to the power from God with Constantine, he was passing the river that lay before his march, which he himself had bridged with boats and well spanned, contriving a device of destruction against himself; 6. of whom it might be said: 'He has dug a pit and hollowed it out, and shall fall into the ditch which he made. His labour shall return upon his own head, and upon his own crown his iniquity shall come down.' 7. Thus indeed, the bridge over the river being broken up, the passage gave way, and all at once the boats sank down into the depth, men and all; and the most impious man himself first, and then also the shield-bearers about him, as the divine oracles foretell, 'sank like lead in the mighty waters'; 8. so that fitly, if not in words yet in deeds, like those about the great servant Moses, those who had won the victory from God might thus, concerning the impious tyrant of old, hymn and say: 'Let us sing to the Lord, for He has been gloriously glorified; horse and rider He has cast into the sea. The Lord is my helper and protector, He has become my salvation,' and, 'Who is like Thee among the gods, O Lord? who is like Thee? glorified among the holy ones, wonderful in glories, doing wonders.' 9. These things, and as many as are akin and like to these, Constantine, by his very deeds hymning to God the supreme Ruler and the Author of the victory, entered Rome in triumph, all at once, together with quite young children and women, receiving him—the members of the senate and the otherwise most distinguished, with the whole people of the Romans—with radiant eyes and very souls, as a redeemer and saviour and benefactor, with acclamations and insatiable joy. But he, possessing as it were an inborn piety toward God, 10. in no way shaken by the shouts nor lifted up by the praises, but well aware of the help from God, straightway ordered a trophy of the saving Passion to be set up under the hand of his own statue; and indeed, when they had set it up in the most public place of Rome holding the saving sign in its right hand, he commanded this very inscription to be set down in these words in the Roman tongue: 11. 'By this saving sign, the true proof of valour, I delivered and freed your city, saved from the yoke of the tyrant; nay more, having freed both the senate and the people of the Romans, I restored them to their ancient renown and splendour.' 12. And indeed thereupon Constantine himself, and with him the emperor Licinius—who had not yet at that time turned aside in mind to the madness into which he afterward fell—propitiating God the Author of all their good things, both of one counsel and mind drew up a most perfect and most complete law on behalf of the Christians; and they sent to Maximinus, who still held power over the nations of the East and made pretence of friendship toward them, the marvellous things that had been done for them by God, and the things of the victory over the tyrant, and the law itself. 13. And he, being as a tyrant grievously pained at what he learned, then, not wishing to seem to yield to others, nor again to put aside what was commanded, from fear of those who commanded it, as though of his own authority for the first time writes perforce this letter on behalf of the Christians to the governors under him, falsely feigning against himself things which he had never yet done.

Copy of the rendering of the tyrant's letter: 'Jovius Maximinus Augustus, to Sabinus. I am persuaded that it is plain both to your gravity and to all men that our masters Diocletian and Maximian, our fathers, when they perceived that well-nigh all men, the worship of the gods being forsaken, had attached themselves to the nation of the Christians, rightly ordained that all men who had withdrawn from the worship of those same immortal gods should be recalled to the worship of the gods by open chastisement and punishment. 2. But when I came happily for the first time to the East, and learned that into certain places very many of the men who were able to be of profit to the public were being banished by the judges for the aforesaid cause, I gave commands to each of the judges that henceforth none of them should deal harshly with the provincials, but rather by flattery and exhortations recall them to the worship of the gods. 3. Then, accordingly, when, in obedience to my command, the things ordained were observed by the judges, it came about that none from the parts of the East was either banished or insulted, but rather, from no grievous thing being done against them, they were recalled to the worship of the gods. 4. But after these things, when in the past year I happily came to Nicomedia and was staying there, citizens of the same city came to me, together with the images of the gods, earnestly entreating that by every means such a nation should in no way be permitted to dwell in their country. 5. But when I learned that very many men of the same worship dwelt in those very parts, I gave them this answer: that I gladly received their request with thanks, but perceived that it was not asked by all; if, then, any persisted in the same superstition, that each one should so hold the will in his own choice, and, if he wished, recognize the worship of the gods. 6. Nevertheless, to the Nicomedians of the same city, and to the other cities which themselves also had so very earnestly made the like request to me—namely, that none of the Christians should dwell in their cities—I had necessarily to answer kindly, because this very thing all the ancient emperors also preserved, and it was pleasing to the gods themselves, through whom all men and the very administration of public affairs subsist; that I would therefore confirm so great a request as they bring forward on behalf of the worship of their deity. 7. Therefore, even though most especially before this time it has been enjoined upon your devotedness by letters, and likewise commanded by ordinances, that nothing harsh be done against the provincials who were diligent to preserve such a custom, but that they be borne with patiently and in moderation, nevertheless, that they may suffer neither insults nor extortions from the beneficiarii nor from any others whatever, I have thought it fitting by these letters too to remind your gravity, that you should rather make our provincials recognize the care of the gods by flatteries and exhortations; 8. whence, if any of his own choice should take up the recognition of the worship of the gods, it is fitting to receive these; but if any wish to follow their own worship, you should leave them in their own power. 9. Wherefore your devotedness ought to preserve what has been entrusted to you, and let power be given to none to wear down our provincials by insults and extortions, since, as has been written above, it is fitting rather by exhortations and flatteries to recall our provincials to the worship of the gods. And that this our command may come to the knowledge of all our provincials, you ought to make known what has been commanded by an edict set forth by you.' 10. Having commanded these things, being forced thereto by necessity, but not ordaining them according to his own purpose, he was no longer true nor trustworthy in the eyes of all, on account of his fickle and lying disposition already before, after the like concession. 11. None of our people, therefore, dared to convene an assembly nor to set himself forth in the open, since not even this did the writing allow him, permitting us only to be kept free from molestation, but not commanding us to hold assemblies nor to build houses of churches nor to do any other of our customary things. 12. And yet the advocates of peace and piety had written to grant him leave for these things, and had conceded them to all under them by proclamations and laws; but the most impious man did not choose to yield in this, save when, driven on by the divine justice, he was at last, unwillingly, brought to it.

But there came upon him a cause of this kind. Unable to bear the greatness of the rule entrusted to him beyond his desert, but, through inexperience of prudent and kingly reasoning, handling affairs tastelessly, and lifted up in soul beyond reason by the boastfulness of pride over all, he was moved to dare to behave insolently even against the partners of his empire, who surpassed him in all things—in birth and nurture and education, in dignity and understanding, and in that most crowning thing of all, prudence and piety toward the true God—and to proclaim himself first in honour. Pushing his madness to the point of frenzy, 2. and having broken the covenant which he had made with Licinius, he raises a truceless war; then, in a short time confounding all things and throwing every city into uproar, and gathering every army, a countless multitude of myriads, he went out to battle, arraying himself against him, lifted up in soul by the hopes of the demons, whom indeed he reckoned gods, and by the myriads of his soldiers. 3. And indeed, when he came to grips, he was left bereft of the oversight from God, the victory being dispensed by the one and only God of all to him who then ruled. First, then, he loses the soldiery in which he had trusted; 4. and when the bodyguards about him had left him stripped and bereft of all, and had fled to the ruler, the wretch, stripping off as quickly as possible the imperial array that did not befit him, cowardly and basely and unmanfully sank himself into the multitude, and then ran away, and, hiding himself about the country and the villages, scarcely escaped the hands of the enemies, procuring his own safety, by his very deeds proving most surely true and faithful the divine oracles, 5. in which it is said: 'A king is not saved by his great power, and a giant shall not be saved by the multitude of his strength; a horse is a vain thing for safety, and in the multitude of his power he shall not be saved. Behold, the eyes of the Lord are upon them that fear Him, that hope in His mercy, to deliver their souls from death.' 6. Thus, then, full of shame, the tyrant came to his own parts, and first, in raging fury, slew many priests and prophets of the gods he had formerly admired—by whose oracles he had been stirred up to take the war—as charlatans and impostors, and above all betrayers of his safety; then, having given glory to the God of the Christians, and ordained a most perfect and complete law on behalf of their freedom, straightway, dying a hard death, no respite of time being granted him, he ended his life. The law he sent down was of this kind: 7. Copy of the rendering of the tyrant's ordinance on behalf of the Christians, translated from the Roman tongue into the Greek: 'The Emperor Caesar Gaius Valerius Maximinus, Germanicus, Sarmaticus, Pious, Fortunate, Invincible, Augustus. That in every way we continually take thought for the advantage of our provincials, and wish to grant them those things by which the interests of all are best set right, and whatsoever pertains to their common advantage and usefulness, and such things as suit the public benefit and are dear to the minds of each—we believe that none is ignorant, but that each man, recurring to the very thing that is done, knows and has it plain within himself. 8. When, therefore, before this it became plain to our knowledge that, on this pretext—on which it had been commanded by the most divine Diocletian and Maximian, our parents, that the assemblies of the Christians should be done away—many extortions and despoilings had been committed by the officials, and that for the future this was advancing against our provincials (of whom we are most zealous that the fitting forethought be taken), their own substance being worn down, we gave letters last year to the governors of each province, and made it law that, if any wished to follow such a custom or the same observance of worship, he should hold to his own purpose unhindered and be impeded and prevented by none, and that there should be liberty for them, without any fear or suspicion, to do that which is pleasing to each. 9. But not even now could it escape us that some of the judges set aside our commands and made our people doubtful concerning our ordinances, and caused them more hesitantly to approach those forms of worship which were pleasing to them. 10. In order, therefore, that for the future all suspicion or ambiguity of fear may be removed, we have made it law that this edict be set forth, that it may be plain to all that it is permitted to those who wish to follow this sect and worship, by this our gift, even as each one wishes or as is pleasant to him, so to approach this worship which he has chosen to observe by custom. And it has been conceded that they may build their own houses of the Lord. 11. And that our gift may be still greater, we have thought it right to ordain this too: that if any houses or lands which formerly belonged of right to the Christians have, by the command of our parents, passed into the right of the fiscus, or been seized by any city—whether a sale of these has been made, or they have been given to anyone as a gift—all these we have ordered to be recalled to the ancient right of the Christians, that in this too all may take perception of our piety and forethought.' 12. These were the utterances of the tyrant, not falling a full year short of his decrees against the Christians set up on pillars; and with him with whom a little before we seemed impious and atheists and the ruin of all life—so that we were permitted to dwell not only in no city, but not even in any country or wilderness—with him now ordinances and laws on behalf of the Christians were drawn up; and those who a little before, by fire and iron and by being made food for beasts and birds, were being destroyed before his eyes, and were enduring most pitiably every kind of chastisement and punishment and departure from life, as atheists and impious—these now are by the same man both acknowledged to practise their worship and permitted to build their houses of the Lord, and the tyrant himself confesses that they have a share in certain rights. 13. And indeed, having made such confessions, as though obtaining some benefit on account of these very things, suffering doubtless less than he ought to have suffered, smitten by a sudden scourge of God, he came to his end in the second engagement of the war; 14. and his overthrow came upon him not such as befell generals and commanders who, often playing the man in war for the sake of valour and of their comrades, bravely undergo a glorious end, but, as an impious man and fighter against God, while his array was still standing before him on the plain, remaining himself at home and hiding, he paid the fitting penalty, smitten by a sudden scourge of God over his whole body, so that, driven by dread pains and agonies, he fell prone, wasted by famine, his whole flesh melted away by an unseen and God-sent fire, so that the whole form of his old appearance dissolved and vanished, and there was left only, as it were, an image of dry bones, like something skeletonized by long time, so that those present could think nothing else than that his body had become the tomb of his soul, which was buried in a corpse already wholly dissolved. 15. And as the heat consumed him yet more violently from the depth of his marrow, his eyes started forth, and falling from their own sockets left him blind; and he, even still breathing upon this, making acknowledgment to the Lord, called for death; and at the very last, confessing that he suffered these things justly for his outrage against Christ, he gave up his soul.

Thus, then, Maximinus being removed out of the way—who, being the only one yet left of the enemies of true religion, appeared the worst of all—the renewal of the churches from the foundations was raised by the grace of God the Almighty, and the word of Christ, shining forth to the glory of the God of all, recovered greater freedom than before, while the impiety of the enemies of true religion was filled with the utmost shame and dishonour. 2. For Maximinus first, himself proclaimed a common enemy of all by the rulers, was inscribed on public proclamations as a most impious and most ill-named and most God-hated tyrant; and as many writings as had been set up in honour of him and his children in every city, some, cast down from on high to the ground, were shattered, and others were made useless, blackened over with a dark colour; and likewise as many statues as had been set up in his honour were in like manner cast down and shattered, lying exposed to the laughter and sport of those who wished to insult and abuse them. 3. Then also all honours of the other enemies of true religion were taken away, and all who held with Maximinus were slain—especially those who, honoured by him with ruling dignities, in their flattery toward him had insolently outraged our word; 4. such as was Peucetius, most honoured and revered by him above all, and most genuine of his comrades, twice consul and thrice consul, and appointed by him prefect of the chief office; and Culcianus likewise, who had advanced through every ruling authority, who too had made himself illustrious with the countless blood of the Christians in Egypt; and besides these not a few others, through whom most of all the tyranny of Maximinus had been strengthened and increased. 5. And justice summoned also Theotecnus, by no means consigning to oblivion the things done by him against the Christians. For on account of the idol set up by him at Antioch, seeming to prosper, he had already been deemed worthy of a governorship by Maximinus; 6. but Licinius, entering the city of the Antiochenes, and making a search for charlatans, tortured the prophets and priests of the newly set up idol, asking by what device they feigned their deceit; and when it was impossible for them, hard pressed by the tortures, to conceal it, and they declared that the whole mystery was a deceit contrived by the art of Theotecnus, he laid upon all the fitting penalty, and gave over first Theotecnus himself, and then also his partners in the sorcery, after very many maltreatments, to death. 7.
